======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Fantasy literature
======================================================================

{{Short description|Literature set in an imaginary universe}}
{{Redirect|Fantasy book|the 1947–1951 magazine|Fantasy Book{{!}}''Fantasy Book''|the 1981–1987 magazine|Fantasy Book (1981 magazine){{!}}''Fantasy Book'' (1981 magazine)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2022}}
[[File:Curdie went on after her, flashing his torch about..jpg|thumb|Illustration from 1920 edition of [[George MacDonald]]'s novel ''[[The Princess and the Goblin]]'']]
{{Fantasy}}{{Speculative fiction sidebar}}
'''Fantasy literature''' is literature set in an [[imaginary universe]], often but not always without any locations, events, or people from the real world. [[magic (paranormal)|Magic]], the [[supernatural]] and [[Legendary creature|magical creatures]] are common in many of these imaginary worlds. Fantasy literature may be directed at both children and adults.

[[Fantasy]] is considered a genre of [[speculative fiction]] and is distinguished from the genres of [[science fiction]] and [[horror fiction|horror]] by the absence of scientific or macabre themes, respectively, though these may overlap. Historically, most works of fantasy were in [[literature|written form]], but since the 1960s, a growing segment of the genre has taken the form of [[fantasy film]]s, [[fantasy television|fantasy television program]]s, [[graphic novel]]s, [[video game]]s, [[music]] and [[art]].

Many fantasy novels originally written for children and adolescents also attract an adult audience. Examples include ''[[Alice's Adventures in Wonderland]]'', the ''[[Harry Potter]]'' series, ''[[The Chronicles of Narnia]]'', and ''[[The Hobbit]]''.

==History==
{{main|History of fantasy|Early history of fantasy}}

===Beginnings===
Stories involving magic and terrible monsters have existed in spoken forms before the advent of printed literature. [[Classical mythology]] is replete with fantastical stories and characters, the best known (and perhaps the most relevant to modern fantasy) being the works of [[Homer]] (Greek) and [[Virgil]] (Roman).<ref name="taproot">John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Taproot texts", p 921 {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref>

The philosophy of [[Plato]] has had great influence on the fantasy genre. In the Christian Platonic tradition, the reality of other worlds, and an overarching structure of great metaphysical and moral importance, has lent substance to the fantasy worlds of modern works.<ref>{{cite book|first =Stephen|last = Prickett|title =Victorian Fantasy|page= 229 |isbn = 0-253-17461-9|publisher = Indiana University Press|date = 1979}}</ref>

With [[Empedocles]] ({{Circa|490|430 BC}}), [[Classical element|element]]s are often used in fantasy works as personifications of the forces of nature.<ref>John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Elemental" p 313-4, {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref>

[[India]] has a long tradition of fantastical stories and characters, dating back to [[Vedic mythology]]. The ''[[Panchatantra]]'' (''Fables of Bidpai''), which some scholars believe was composed around the 3rd century BC.<ref>{{Harvnb|Jacobs|1888}}, Introduction, page xv; {{Harvnb|Ryder|1925}}, Translator's introduction, quoting Hertel: "the original work was composed in Kashmir, about 200 B.C. At this date, however, many of the individual stories were already ancient."</ref> It is based on older oral traditions, including "animal fables that are as old as we are able to imagine".<ref>[http://www.i-c-r.org.uk/publications/monographarchive/Monograph36.pdf  Doris Lessing, ''Problems, Myths and Stories''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160509185027/http://www.i-c-r.org.uk/publications/monographarchive/Monograph36.pdf |date=2016-05-09 }}, London: Institute for Cultural Research Monograph Series No. 36, 1999, p 13</ref>

It was influential in Europe and the [[Middle East]]. It used various animal [[fable]]s and magical tales to illustrate the central Indian principles of [[political science]]. Talking animals endowed with human qualities have now become a staple of modern fantasy.<ref>Richard Matthews (2002). ''Fantasy: The Liberation of Imagination'', p. 8-10. [[Routledge]]. {{ISBN|0-415-93890-2}}.</ref>

The ''[[Baital Pachisi]]'' (''Vikram and the Vampire''), a collection of various fantasy tales set within a [[frame story]] is, according to [[Richard Francis Burton]] and [[Isabel Burton]], "the germ which culminated in the ''[[The Book of One Thousand and One Nights|Arabian Nights]]'', and which also inspired the ''[[Golden Ass]]'' of [[Apuleius]], (2nd century A.D). [[Giovanni Boccaccio|Boccaccio]]'s ''[[The Decameron|Decamerone]]'' (c.1353) the ''[[Pentamerone]]'' (1634, 1636) and all that class of facetious fictitious literature."<ref>[[Isabel Burton]], [http://www.sacred-texts.com/goth/vav/vav02.htm Preface] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170521214449/http://www.sacred-texts.com/goth/vav/vav02.htm |date=21 May 2017 }}, in [[Richard Francis Burton]] (1870), ''Vikram and The Vampire''.</ref>

''[[The Book of One Thousand and One Nights]] (Arabian Nights)'' from the [[Middle East]] has been influential in the West since it was translated from the Arabic into French in 1704 by [[Antoine Galland]].<ref>[[L. Sprague de Camp]], ''[[Literary Swordsmen and Sorcerers]]: The Makers of Heroic Fantasy'', p 10 {{ISBN|0-87054-076-9}}</ref> Many imitations were written, especially in France.<ref name="arabianNights2">John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Arabian fantasy", p 52 {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref>

The [[Fornaldarsaga]]s, [[Norse saga|Norse]] and [[Iceland]]ic [[saga]]s, both of which are based on ancient [[oral tradition]] influenced the German Romantics, as well as [[William Morris]], and [[J. R. R. Tolkien]].<ref name="nordic">John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Nordic fantasy", p 692 {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref> The [[Anglo-Saxon]] epic poem ''[[Beowulf]]'' has also had deep influence on the fantasy genre; although it was unknown for centuries and so not developed in medieval legend and romance, several fantasy works have retold the tale, such as [[John Champlin Gardner Jr.|John Gardner]]'s ''[[Grendel]]''.<ref>John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Beowulf", p 107 {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref>

[[Celtic mythology|Celtic folklore]] and legend has been an inspiration for many fantasy works.<ref name="celtic">John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Celtic fantasy", p 275 {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref>

The [[Wales|Welsh]] tradition has been particularly influential, owing to its connection to King Arthur and its collection in a single work, the epic [[Mabinogion]].<ref name="celtic" />  One influential retelling of this was the fantasy work of [[Evangeline Walton]].<ref>Michael Moorcock, ''Wizardry & Wild Romance: A Study of Epic Fantasy'' p 101 {{ISBN|1-932265-07-4}}</ref> The Irish [[Ulster Cycle]] and [[Fenian Cycle]] have also been plentifully mined for fantasy.<ref name="celtic" /> Its greatest influence was, however, indirect.  Celtic folklore and mythology provided a major source for the Arthurian cycle of [[chivalric romance]]:  the [[Matter of Britain]]. Although the subject matter was heavily reworked by the authors, these romances developed marvels until they became independent of the original folklore and fictional, an important stage in the development of fantasy.<ref>Colin Manlove, ''Christian Fantasy:  from 1200 to the Present'' p 12 {{ISBN|0-268-00790-X}}</ref>

{{Literature}}

===From the 13th century===
Romance or [[chivalric romance]] is a type of [[prose]] and [[Verse (poetry)|verse]] [[narrative]] that reworked [[legend]]s, [[fairy tale]]s, and history to suit the readers' and hearers' tastes, but by {{Circa|1600}} they were out of fashion, and [[Miguel de Cervantes]] famously [[burlesque]]d them in his novel ''[[Don Quixote]]''. Still, [[Medievalism|the modern image of "medieval"]] is more influenced by the romance than by any other medieval genre, and the word ''medieval'' evokes knights, distressed damsels, dragons, and other romantic tropes.<ref>{{cite book|author-link=C. S. Lewis|first = C. S.|last = Lewis|title = [[The Discarded Image]]|page= 9 |isbn = 0-521-47735-2|publisher = Cambridge University Press|date= 1994}}</ref>

===Renaissance===
At the time of the [[Renaissance]] romance continued to be popular, and the trend was to more fantastic fiction. The English ''[[Le Morte d'Arthur]]'' by [[Sir Thomas Malory]] (c.1408–1471) was written in prose, and the work dominates the Arthurian literature.<ref>[[John Grant (author)|John Grant]] and [[John Clute]], ''[[The Encyclopedia of Fantasy]]'', "Malory, (Sir) Thomas" p 621, {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref> Arthurian motifs have appeared steadily in literature from its publication, though the works have been a mix of fantasy and non-fantasy works.<ref>John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Arthur" p 60-1, {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref> At the time, it and the Spanish ''[[Amadis de Gaula]]'' (1508), which was also written in prose, spawned many imitators, and the genre was popularly well-received. It later produced such masterpieces of Renaissance poetry as [[Ludovico Ariosto]]'s ''Orlando furioso'' and [[Torquato Tasso]]'s ''Gerusalemme Liberata''. Ariosto's tale in particular was a source text for many fantasies of adventure.<ref>John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Ariosto, Lodovico" p 60-1, {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref>

During the [[Renaissance]], [[Giovanni Francesco Straparola]] wrote and published ''[[The Facetious Nights of Straparola]]'' (1550–1555), a collection of stories of which many are literary [[fairy tale]]s. [[Giambattista Basile]] wrote and published the ''[[Pentamerone]]'', which was the first collection of stories to contain solely what would later be known as fairy tales. The two works include the oldest recorded form of many well-known (and some more obscure) European fairy tales.<ref>Steven Swann Jones, ''The Fairy Tale: The Magic Mirror of Imagination'', Twayne Publishers, New York, 1995, {{ISBN|0-8057-0950-9}}, p38</ref> This was the beginning of a tradition that would both influence the fantasy genre and be incorporated in it, as many works of [[fairytale fantasy]] appear to this day.<ref>L. Sprague de Camp, ''Literary Swordsmen and Sorcerers: The Makers of Heroic Fantasy'', p 11 {{ISBN|0-87054-076-9}}</ref>

In a work on [[alchemy]] in the 16th century, [[Paracelsus]] (1493–1541) identified four types of beings with the four elements of alchemy: [[gnome]]s (earth elementals); [[Ondine (mythology)|undine]]s (water); [[sylph]]s (air); and [[salamander (legendary creature)|salamanders]] (fire).<ref>Carole B. Silver, ''Strange and Secret Peoples: Fairies and Victorian Consciousness'', p 38 {{ISBN|0-19-512199-6}}</ref>  Most of these beings are found in folklore as well as alchemy, and their names are often used interchangeably with similar beings from folklore.<ref>[[C.S. Lewis]], ''[[The Discarded Image]]'', p135 {{ISBN|0-521-47735-2}}</ref>

===Enlightenment===
Literary fairy tales, such as those written by [[Charles Perrault]] (1628–1703) and [[Madame d'Aulnoy]] (c.1650 – 1705), became very popular early in the [[Age of Enlightenment]].  Many of Perrault's tales became fairy tale staples and were influential to later fantasy.  When d'Aulnoy termed her works ''contes de fée'' (fairy tales), she invented the term that is now generally used for the genre, thus distinguishing such tales from those involving no marvels.<ref>Jack Zipes, ''The Great Fairy Tale Tradition: From Straparola and Basile to the Brothers Grimm'', p 858, {{ISBN|0-393-97636-X}}</ref> This approach influenced later writers who took up the folk fairy tales in the same manner during the [[Romanticism|Romantic era]].<ref name="SpragueP9-11">[[L. Sprague de Camp]], ''[[Literary Swordsmen and Sorcerers]]: The Makers of Heroic Fantasy'', p 9-11 {{ISBN|0-87054-076-9}}</ref>

Several fantasies aimed at an adult readership were also published in 18th century France, including [[Voltaire]]'s
"[[philosophical fiction|contes philosophique]]"  ''The Princess of Babylon'' (1768) and ''The White Bull'' (1774).<ref>[[Brian Stableford]], ''The A to Z of Fantasy Literature'', p xx, Scarecrow Press, Plymouth. 2005.  {{ISBN|0-8108-6829-6}}</ref> This era, however, was notably hostile to fantasy. Writers of the new types of fiction such as [[Daniel Defoe|Defoe]], [[Samuel Richardson|Richardson]], and [[Henry Fielding|Fielding]] were realistic in style, and many early realistic works were critical of fantastical elements in fiction.<ref>[[Lin Carter]], ed. ''Realms of Wizardry'' p xiii–xiv Doubleday and Company Garden City, NY, 1976</ref>

However, in the [[Elizabethan era]] in [[England]], fantasy literature became extraordinarily popular and fueled [[Populism|populist]] and [[Anti-authoritarianism|anti-authoritarian]] sentiment during the [[1590s in England|1590s]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Schama |first=Simon |title=A History of Britain 1: 3000 BC-AD 1603 At the Edge of the World? |title-link=A History of Britain (TV series)#DVDs and books |publisher=[[BBC Worldwide]] |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-563-48714-2 |edition=Paperback 2003 |location=London |pages=390 |author-link=Simon Schama}}</ref> Topics that were written about included "[[fairy]]lands in which the sexes traded places [and] men and immortals mingl[ing]".<ref name=":0" />

===Romanticism===
[[Romanticism]], a movement of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century, was a dramatic reaction to rationalism, challenging the priority of reason and promoting the importance of imagination and spirituality.  Its success in rehabilitating imagination was of fundamental importance to the evolution of fantasy, and its interest in medieval [[Romance (heroic literature)|romances]] provided many motifs to modern fantasy.<ref>John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Romanticism", p 821 {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref>

The Romantics invoked the medieval romance as a model for the works they wanted to produce, in contrast to the realism of the Enlightenment.<ref>John Grant and John Clute, ''The Encyclopedia of Fantasy'', "Romance", p 821 {{ISBN|0-312-19869-8}}</ref> One of the first literary results of this trend was the [[Gothic novel]], a genre that began in Britain with ''[[The Castle of Otranto]]'' (1764) by [[Horace Walpole]]. That work is considered the predecessor to both modern fantasy and modern [[horror fiction]].<ref name="SpragueP9-11"/> Another noted Gothic novel which also contains a large amount of [[One Thousand and One Nights|Arabian Nights]]-influenced fantasy elements is ''[[Vathek]]'' (1786) by [[William Thomas Beckford]].<ref>Brian Stableford, ''The A to Z of Fantasy Literature'', p 40, Scarecrow Press, Plymouth. 2005.  {{ISBN|0-8108-6829-6}}</ref>
[[File:Brothers Grimm Blow.jpg|thumb|The Grimm brothers.]]
In the later part of the Romantic period, folklorists collected folktales, epic poems, and ballads, and released them in printed form. The [[Brothers Grimm]] were inspired by the movement of [[German Romanticism]] in their 1812 collection ''[[Grimm's Fairy Tales]]'', and they in turn inspired other collectors.  Frequently their motivation stemmed not merely from Romanticism, but from [[Romantic nationalism]], in that many were inspired to save their own country's folklore. Sometimes, as in the ''[[Kalevala]]'', they compiled existing folklore into an epic to match other nation's, and sometimes, as in ''[[Ossian|The Poems of Ossian]]'', they fabricated folklore that should have been there.  These works, whether fairy tale, ballads, or folk epics, were a major source for later fantasy works.<ref name="Michael Moorcock p 35">Michael Moorcock, ''Wizardry & Wild Romance: A Study of Epic Fantasy'' p 35 {{ISBN|1-932265-07-4}}</ref>

The Romantic interest in medievalism also resulted in a revival of interest in the literary fairy tale. The tradition begun with [[Giovanni Francesco Straparola]] and [[Giambattista Basile]] and developed by [[Charles Perrault]] and the French [[précieuses]] was taken up by the German Romantic movement. The German author [[Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué]] created medieval-set stories such as ''[[Undine (novella)|Undine]]'' (1811), ''[[The Magic Ring]]'' (1812) and ''Sintram and his Companions'' (1815), which would later inspire British writers such as [[George MacDonald]] and [[William Morris]].<ref>
[[Brian Stableford]], "Undine", (pp. 1992–1994). in [[Frank N. Magill]], ed. ''Survey of Modern Fantasy Literature'', Vol 4. Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Salem Press, Inc., 1983.  {{ISBN|0-89356-450-8}}</ref><ref>[[Mike Ashley (writer)|Mike Ashley]], 
"Fouqué, Friedrich (Heinrich Karl),(Baron) de la Motte",(p. 654-5) in ''St. James Guide To Fantasy Writers'', edited by [[David Pringle]]. St. James Press, 1996. {{ISBN|1-55862-205-5}}</ref><ref>Veronica Ortenberg, ''In Search of the Holy Grail: The Quest for the Middle Ages'',
(38–9) Continuum International Publishing Group, 2006, {{ISBN|1-85285-383-2}}.</ref> 
[[E.T.A. Hoffmann]]'s tales, such as ''[[The Golden Pot]]'' (1814) and ''[[The Nutcracker and the Mouse King]]'' (1816) were notable additions to the canon of German fantasy.<ref>Penrith Goff, "E.T.A. Hoffmann", (pp.111–120) in E. F. Bleiler, ''Supernatural Fiction Writers: Fantasy and Horror''. New York: Scribner's, 1985.  {{ISBN|0-684-17808-7}}</ref> [[Ludwig Tieck]]'s collection ''Phantasus'' (1812–1817) contained several short fairy tales, including "The Elves".<ref>D. P Haase, "Ludwig Tieck" (pp.83–90), in E. F. Bleiler, ''Supernatural Fiction Writers: Fantasy and Horror''. New York: Scribner's, 1985.  {{ISBN|0-684-17808-7}}</ref>

In France, the main writers of Romantic-era fantasy were [[Charles Nodier]] with ''Smarra'' (1821) and ''Trilby'' (1822)<ref>Franz Rottensteiner, ''The Fantasy Book:an illustrated history from Dracula to Tolkien'' (p. 137) Collier Books, 1978. {{ISBN|0-02-053560-0}}</ref><ref>A. Richard Oliver, ''Charles Nodier:Pilot of Romanticism''. (p. 134-37) Syracuse University Press, 1964.</ref> and [[Théophile Gautier]] who penned such stories as "Omphale" (1834) and "[[One of Cleopatra's Nights and Other Fantastic Romances|One of Cleopatra's Nights]]" (1838) as well as the novel ''Spirite'' (1866).<ref>Brian Stableford, ''The A to Z of Fantasy Literature'' (p. 159), Scarecrow Press, Plymouth. 2005.  {{ISBN|0-8108-6829-6}}</ref><ref>Brian Stableford, "Théophile Gautier", (pp. 45–50) in E. F. Bleiler, ''Supernatural Fiction Writers: Fantasy and Horror''. New York: Scribner's, 1985.  {{ISBN|0-684-17808-7}}</ref>

===Victorian era===
Fantasy literature was popular in [[Victorian literature|Victorian times]], with the works of writers such as [[Mary Shelley]], William Morris, George MacDonald, and [[Charles Lutwidge Dodgson|Charles Dodgson]] reaching wider audiences.

[[Hans Christian Andersen]] took a new approach to fairy tales by creating original stories told in a serious fashion.<ref name="PrickettP66-67">{{cite book|first = Stephen |last= Prickett|title=Victorian Fantasy|pages=66–67 |isbn=0-253-17461-9|publisher=Indiana University Press|date=1979}}</ref>  From this origin, [[John Ruskin]] wrote ''[[The King of the Golden River]]'' (1851), a fairy tale that included complex levels of characterization and created in the Southwest Wind an irascible but kindly character similar to [[J.R.R. Tolkien]]'s later [[Gandalf]].<ref name="PrickettP66-67"/>

The history of modern fantasy literature began with [[George MacDonald]],  author of such novels as ''[[The Princess and the Goblin]]'' (1868) and ''[[Phantastes]]'' (1868), the latter of which is widely considered to be the first fantasy novel written for adults. MacDonald also wrote one of the first critical essays about the fantasy genre, "The Fantastic Imagination", in his book ''A Dish of Orts'' (1893).<ref>George MacDonald, "The Fantastic Imagination". Reprinted in Boyer, Robert H. and Zahorski, Kenneth J. ''Fantasists on Fantasy''. New York: Avon Discus, 1984. pp. 11–22, {{ISBN|0-380-86553-X}}</ref><ref name="scholes">{{cite book|author-link = Robert Scholes|first = Robert|last = Scholes|chapter = Boiling Roses|editor1-first= George E. |editor1-last=Slusser|editor2-first = Eric S.|editor2-last = Rabkin|title = Intersections: Fantasy and Science Fiction|location = Carbondale|publisher= Southern Illinois University Press|date = 1987|isbn = 080931374X|pages =3–18}}</ref> MacDonald was a major influence on both Tolkien and [[C. S. Lewis]].<ref>[[Gary K. Wolfe]], "George MacDonald", pp. 239–246 in Bleiler, E. F., ed. ''Supernatural Fiction Writers''. New York: Scribner's, 1985. {{ISBN|0-684-17808-7}}</ref>

The other major fantasy author of this era was William Morris, an admirer of the [[Middle Ages]] and a poet who wrote several fantastic romances and novels in the latter part of the 19th century, including ''[[The Well at the World's End]]'' (1896).  Morris was inspired by the medieval sagas, and his writing was deliberately archaic in the style of the [[chivalric romance]]s.<ref name="CarterP2">Lin Carter, ed. ''Realms of Wizardry'' p 2 Doubleday and Company Garden City, NY, 1976</ref>  Morris's work represented an important milestone in the history of fantasy, as while other writers wrote of foreign lands or of [[dream world (plot device)|dream world]]s, Morris was the first to set his stories in an entirely [[fantasy world|invented world]].<ref name="Lin Carter p 39">Lin Carter, ed. ''Kingdoms of Sorcery'', p 39 Doubleday and Company Garden City, NY, 1976</ref>

Authors such as [[Edgar Allan Poe]] and [[Oscar Wilde]] also contributed to the development of fantasy with their writing of horror stories.<ref>Stephen Prickett, ''Victorian Fantasy'' p 98-9 {{ISBN|0-253-17461-9}}</ref> Wilde also wrote a large number of children's fantasies, collected in ''The Happy Prince and Other Stories'' (1888) and ''A House of Pomegranates'' (1891).<ref>M. J. Elkins, "Oscar Wilde" in E. F. Bleiler, ed. ''Supernatural Fiction Writers''. New York: Scribner's, 1985. (pp.345–350). {{ISBN|0-684-17808-7}}</ref> [[H. Rider Haggard]] developed the conventions of the [[Lost World (genre)|lost world]] subgenre with his novel ''[[King Solomon's Mines]]'' (1885),  which presented a fantastical Africa to a European audience still unfamiliar with the continent.<ref name="CarterP64">Lin Carter, ed. ''Realms of Wizardry'' p 64 Doubleday and Company Garden City, NY, 1976</ref> Other writers, including [[Edgar Rice Burroughs]] and [[Abraham Merritt]], further developed the style.

Several classic [[juvenile fantasy|children's fantasies]] such as [[Lewis Carroll]]'s ''[[Alice's Adventures in Wonderland]]'' (1865),<ref>[[J.R. Pfeiffer]], "Lewis Carroll", p 247-54, in [[E. F. Bleiler]], ''Supernatural Fiction Writers: Fantasy and Horror''. Scribner's, New York, 1985 {{ISBN|0-684-17808-7}}</ref> [[L. Frank Baum]]'s ''[[The Wonderful Wizard of Oz]]'' (1900), as well as the work of [[E. Nesbit]] and [[Frank R. Stockton]] were also published around this time.<ref>Brian Stableford, ''The A to Z of Fantasy Literature'', p 70-3, Scarecrow Press, Plymouth. 2005.  {{ISBN|0-8108-6829-6}}</ref> [[C. S. Lewis]] noted that in the earlier part of the 20th century, fantasy was more accepted in juvenile literature, and therefore a writer interested in fantasy often wrote for that audience, despite using concepts and themes that could form a work aimed at adults.<ref>C. S. Lewis, "On Juvenile Tastes", p 41, ''Of Other Worlds: Essays and Stories'', {{ISBN|0-15-667897-7}}</ref>

At this time, the terminology for the genre was not settled.  Many fantasies in this era were termed fairy tales, including [[Max Beerbohm]]'s "[[The Happy Hypocrite]]" (1896) and MacDonald's ''Phantastes''.<ref>W.R. Irwin, ''The Game of the Impossible'', p 92-3, University of Illinois Press, Urbana Chicago London, 1976</ref> It was not until 1923 that the term "fantasist" was used to describe a writer (in this case, Oscar Wilde) who wrote fantasy fiction.<ref>The term was referenced in a supplement to the ''[[Oxford English Dictionary]]''. See Michael W. McClintock, "High Tech and High Sorcery: Some Discriminations Between Science Fiction and Fantasy", in George E. Slusser, and Eric S. Rabkin, ed., ''Intersections: Fantasy and Science Fiction''. Carbondale: Southern Illinois University Press, 1987.{{ISBN|080931374X}} (pp.26–35.).</ref> The name "fantasy" was not developed until later; as late as J.R.R. Tolkien's ''[[The Hobbit]]'' (1937), the term "fairy tale" was still being used.

===After 1901===
An important factor in the development of the fantasy genre was the arrival of magazines devoted to fantasy fiction. The first such publication was the German magazine ''[[Der Orchideengarten]]'' which ran from 1919 to 1921.<ref>"Orchideengarten, Der". in: M.B. Tymn and [[Mike Ashley (writer)|Mike Ashley]], ''Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Weird Fiction Magazines''. Westport: Greenwood, 1985. pp. 866.
{{ISBN|0-313-21221-X}}</ref> In 1923, the first English-language fantasy fiction magazine, ''[[Weird Tales]]'', was created.<ref>[[Robert Weinberg (author)|Robert Weinberg]], ''The  Weird Tales Story'', Wildside Press, 1999. {{ISBN|1-58715-101-4}}</ref> Many other similar magazines eventually followed.<ref>"Unknown". in: M.B. Tymn and Mike Ashley, ''Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Weird Fiction Magazines''. Westport: Greenwood, 1985. pp. 694–698. {{ISBN|0-313-21221-X}}</ref> and ''[[The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction]]''<ref>Thomas D. Clareson, "Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction" in M.B. Tymn and Mike Ashley, ''Science Fiction, Fantasy, and Weird Fiction Magazines''. Westport: Greenwood, 1985. (pp. 377–391). {{ISBN|0-313-21221-X}}</ref>

[[H. P. Lovecraft]] was deeply influenced by Edgar Allan Poe and to a somewhat lesser extent, by Lord Dunsany;  with his [[Cthulhu Mythos]] stories, he became one of the most influential writers of fantasy and horror in the 20th century.<ref>L. Sprague de Camp, ''Literary Swordsmen and Sorcerers: The Makers of Heroic Fantasy'', p. 79 {{ISBN|0-87054-076-9}}</ref>

Despite MacDonald's future influence, and Morris' popularity at the time, it was not until around the start of the 20th century that fantasy fiction began to reach a large audience, with authors such as [[Lord Dunsany]] (1878–1957) who, following Morris's example, wrote fantasy novels, but also in the short story form.<ref name="CarterP2"/>  He was particularly noted for his vivid and evocative style.<ref name="CarterP2"/>  His style greatly influenced many writers, not always happily; [[Ursula K. Le Guin]], in her essay on style in fantasy "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie", wryly referred to Lord Dunsany as the "First Terrible Fate that Awaiteth Unwary Beginners in Fantasy", alluding to young writers attempting to write in Lord Dunsany's style.<ref>Ursula K. Le Guin, "[[From Elfland to Poughkeepsie]]", pp. 78–79 ''The Language of the Night'' {{ISBN|0-425-05205-2}}</ref> According to [[S. T. Joshi]], "Dunsany's work had the effect of segregating fantasy—a mode whereby the author creates his own realm of pure imagination—from supernatural horror. From the foundations he established came the later work of [[E. R. Eddison]], [[Mervyn Peake]], and J. R. R. Tolkien.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fOyVgu1qElAC&dq=Dunsany%27s+work+had+the+effect+of+segregating+fantasy&pg=PR15 |title=21st-Century Gothic: Great Gothic Novels Since 2000 |isbn=9780810877290 |access-date=15 March 2023 |archive-date=12 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230712072254/https://books.google.com/books?id=fOyVgu1qElAC&dq=Dunsany%27s+work+had+the+effect+of+segregating+fantasy&pg=PR15 |url-status=live |last1=Olson |first1=Danel |date=29 December 2010 |publisher=Scarecrow Press }}</ref>

In Britain in the aftermath of World War I, a notably large number of fantasy books aimed at an adult readership were published, including  ''Living Alone'' (1919) by [[Stella Benson]],<ref name="re">Brian Stableford, " Re-Enchantment in the Aftermath of War", in Stableford, '' Gothic Grotesques: Essays on Fantastic Literature''. Wildside Press, 2009, {{ISBN|978-1-4344-0339-1}}</ref> ''[[A Voyage to Arcturus]]'' (1920) by  [[David Lindsay (novelist)|David Lindsay]],<ref>"David Lindsay" by Gary K. Wolfe, (pp. 541–548) in E. F. Bleiler, ed. ''Supernatural Fiction Writers''. New York: Scribner's, 1985.  {{ISBN|0-684-17808-7}}</ref> ''[[Lady into Fox]]'' (1922) by [[David Garnett]],<ref name="re" /> ''[[Lud-in-the-Mist]]'' (1926) by [[Hope Mirrlees]],<ref name="re" /><ref>E.L. Chapman, "Lud-in-the-Mist", in Frank N. Magill, ed. ''Survey of Modern Fantasy Literature'', Vol. 2. Englewood Cliffs, NJ: Salem Press, Inc., 1983. {{ISBN|0-89356-450-8}}. pp. 926–931.</ref> and ''[[Lolly Willowes]]'' (1926) by [[Sylvia Townsend Warner]].<ref name="re" /><ref>[[Robin Anne Reid]], ''Women in Science Fiction and Fantasy'' (p.39), ABC-CLIO, 2009 {{ISBN|0313335915}}.</ref> [[E. R. Eddison]] was another influential writer who wrote during this era.  He drew inspiration from Northern sagas, as Morris did, but his prose style was modeled more on Tudor and Elizabethan English, and his stories were filled with vigorous characters in glorious adventures.<ref name="Lin Carter p 39"/> Eddison's most famous work is ''[[The Worm Ouroboros]]'' (1922), a long heroic fantasy set on an imaginary version of the planet Mercury.<ref>Michael Moorcock, ''Wizardry & Wild Romance: A Study of Epic Fantasy'' p 47 {{ISBN|1-932265-07-4}}</ref>

Literary critics of the era began to take an interest in "fantasy" as a genre of writing, and also to argue that it was a genre worthy of serious consideration. [[Herbert Read]] devoted a chapter of his book ''English Prose Style'' (1928) to discussing "Fantasy" as an aspect of literature, arguing it was unjustly considered suitable only for children: "The Western World does not seem to have conceived the necessity of Fairy Tales for Grown-Ups".<ref name="scholes" />

In 1938, with the publication of ''[[The Sword in the Stone (novel)|The Sword in the Stone]]'', [[T. H. White]] introduced one of the most notable works of [[comic fantasy]].<ref>Lin Carter, ed. ''Kingdoms of Sorcery'', p 121-2 Doubleday and Company Garden City, NY, 1976</ref>

The first major contribution to the genre after World War II was [[Mervyn Peake]]'s ''[[Titus Groan]]'' (1946), the book that launched the [[Gormenghast (series)|Gormenghast series]]. [[J. R. R. Tolkien]] played a large role in the popularization and accessibility of the fantasy genre with his highly successful publications ''[[The Hobbit]]'' (1937) and ''[[The Lord of the Rings]]'' (1954–55).<ref name=Maggio>{{cite journal |title=There and Back Again: Tolkien's ''The Lord of the Rings'' in the Modern Fiction |first1=Sandra |last1=Sirangelo Maggio |first2=Valter Henrique |last2=Fritsch |journal=Recorte: Revista Eletrônica |volume=8 |issue=2 |year=2011 |url=http://revistas.unincor.br/index.php/recorte/article/view/326/pdf_1 |access-date=July 7, 2012 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304081536/http://revistas.unincor.br/index.php/recorte/article/view/326/pdf_1 |url-status=live }}</ref> Tolkien was largely influenced by an ancient body of [[Anglo-Saxon polytheism|Anglo-Saxon myths]], particularly ''[[Beowulf]]'', as well as William Morris's romances and [[E. R. Eddison]]'s 1922 novel, ''[[The Worm Ouroboros]]''. Tolkien's close friend [[C. S. Lewis]], author of ''[[The Chronicles of Narnia]]'' (1950–56) and a fellow English professor with a similar array of interests, also helped to publicize the fantasy genre. [[Tove Jansson]], author of ''[[Moomins#List of books|The Moomins]]'', was also a strong contributor to the popularity of fantasy literature in the field of children and adults.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-26529309 |title=Tove Jansson: Love, war and the Moomins |work=BBC News |date=13 March 2014 |access-date=28 April 2020 |archive-date=13 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170413015545/http://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-26529309 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Sanderson, Erikson, Brooks, Reeve and Kahn - Lucca Comics & Games 2016.jpg|thumb|Fantasy writers [[Brandon Sanderson]], [[Steven Erikson]], [[Terry Brooks]], [[Philip Reeve]] and [[Joshua Kahn]] at [[Lucca Comics & Games]] 2016]]
The tradition established by these predecessors of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries has continued to thrive and be adapted by new authors. The [[Tolkien's influence on fantasy|influence of J.R.R. Tolkien's fiction]] has—particularly over the genre of [[high fantasy]]—prompted a reaction.<ref>Fornet-Ponse, Thomas. Tolkien's Influence on Fantasy: Interdisziplinäres Seminar Der DTG 27. Bis 29. April 2012, Jena = Tolkiens Einfluss Auf Die Moderne Fantasy. Vol. 9. Düsseldorf: Scriptorium Oxoniae., n.d. Print.</ref>

In China, the idea of fantasy literature as a distinct genre first became prevalent in the early 21st century.<ref name=":Reinders">{{Cite book |last=Reinders |first=Eric |title=Reading Tolkien in Chinese: Religion, Fantasy, and Translation |date=2024 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] Academic |isbn=9781350374645 |series=Perspectives on Fantasy series |location=London, UK}}</ref>{{Rp|page=42}} China has long had pre-genre stories with fantastical elements, including ''[[Zhiguai xiaoshuo|zhiguai]]'', ghost stories, and miracle tales, among others.<ref name=":Reinders" />{{Rp|page=42}} Similarly, fantasy novels in the style of Anglophone fantasy emerged in Arabic literature in the 2010s, beginning with Islām Idrīs's ''[['Usṭūra series|ʔusṭūra]]'' ("legend") series.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web |last=Al Noman |first=Noura |date=2015-01-16 |title=Possibilities and Pitfalls: Building a Fantasy Series in Arabic |url=https://arablit.org/2015/01/16/building-a-fantasy-series-in-arabic/ |access-date=2025-10-26 |website=ARABLIT & ARABLIT QUARTERLY |language=en-US}}</ref>

It is not uncommon for fantasy novels to be ranked on [[The New York Times Best Seller list|''The New York Times'' Best Seller list]], and some have been at number one on the list, including most recently, [[Brandon Sanderson]] in 2014,<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/17/books/brandon-sanderson-tops-best-sellers-with-words-of-radiance.html Brandon Sanderson tops best sellers list with Words of Radiance] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170818040340/https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/17/books/brandon-sanderson-tops-best-sellers-with-words-of-radiance.html |date=18 August 2017 }} April 17, 2014</ref> [[Neil Gaiman]] in 2013,<ref name="NYT 2013-07-07">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/best-sellers-books/2013-07-07/hardcover-fiction/list.html|title=Best-Seller Lists: Hardcover Fiction|date=7 July 2013|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=15 August 2013|archive-date=12 July 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130712043155/http://www.nytimes.com/best-sellers-books/2013-07-07/hardcover-fiction/list.html|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Patrick Rothfuss]]<ref name="NYTBSL 2011-03-20">{{cite web|url=http://www.hawes.com/2011/2011-03-20.pdf|title=' 'The New York Times ' ' Best Seller list: March 20, 2011|publisher=Hawes.com|access-date=November 16, 2011|archive-date=5 October 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111005093043/http://www.hawes.com/2011/2011-03-20.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> and [[George R. R. Martin]] in 2011,<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/best-sellers-books/2011-07-31/overview.html |title=New York Times bestseller list |access-date=July 24, 2011 |work=[[The New York Times]] |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304203555/http://www.nytimes.com/best-sellers-books/2011-07-31/overview.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and [[Terry Goodkind]] in 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hawes.com/2006/2006-08-06.pdf|title=Hawes' archive of ''New York Times'' bestsellers&nbsp;— Week of January 23, 2005|access-date=6 April 2011|archive-date=3 April 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180403051431/http://www.hawes.com/2006/2006-08-06.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Style==

Symbolism often plays a significant role in fantasy literature, often through the use of archetypal figures inspired by earlier texts or [[folklore]]. Some argue that fantasy literature and its archetypes fulfill a function for individuals and society and the messages are continually updated for current societies.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.mcfarlandpub.com/book-2.php?id=978-0-7864-6039-7 |title=Indick, William. Ancient Symbology in Fantasy Literature: A Psychological Study. Jefferson: McFarland &, 2012. Print. |access-date=2013-04-04 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130629202403/http://www.mcfarlandpub.com/book-2.php?id=978-0-7864-6039-7 |archive-date=2013-06-29 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

[[Ursula K. Le Guin]], in her essay "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie", presented the idea that language is the most crucial element of [[high fantasy]], because it creates a sense of place. She analyzed the misuse of a formal, "olden-day" style, saying that it was a dangerous trap for fantasy writers because it was ridiculous when done wrong. She warns writers away from trying to base their style on that of masters such as [[Lord Dunsany]] and [[E. R. Eddison]],<ref>Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie", p 74-5 ''The Language of the Night'' {{ISBN|0-425-05205-2}}</ref> emphasizing that language that is too bland or simplistic creates the impression that the fantasy setting is simply a modern world in disguise, and presents examples of clear, effective fantasy writing in brief excerpts from [[Tolkien]] and [[Evangeline Walton]].<ref>Ursula K. Le Guin, "From Elfland to Poughkeepsie", pp. 78–80 ''The Language of the Night'' {{ISBN|0-425-05205-2}}</ref>

[[Michael Moorcock]] observed that many writers use archaic language for its sonority and to lend color to a lifeless story.<ref name="Michael Moorcock p 35"/> Brian Peters writes that in various forms of [[fairytale fantasy]], even the villain's language might be inappropriate if vulgar.<ref>Alec Austin, [http://www.strangehorizons.com/2002/20020624/epic_fantasy.shtml "Quality in Epic Fantasy"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140808040720/http://www.strangehorizons.com/2002/20020624/epic_fantasy.shtml |date=2014-08-08 }}.  The generic features of historical fantasy literature, as a mode of inverting the real (including nineteenth-century ghost stories, children's stories, city comedies, classical dreams, stories of highway women, and Edens) are discussed in ''Writing and Fantasy'', ed. Ceri Sullivan and Barbara White (London: Longman, 1999)</ref>
