|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w5YMEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA80}}</ref>
==== Digital ====
{{Further|Mind uploading in fiction}}
A common theme in [[cyberpunk]] is [[digital immortality]], achieved by [[Mind uploading|transferring a person's consciousness to a computer]].<ref name="GreenwoodEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="Fischer" /> One version of this concept involves the uploaded mind being conscious inside the machine, as in [[William Gibson]]'s [[Sprawl trilogy]] starting with the 1984 novel ''[[Neuromancer]]''.<ref name="StephenWebbImmortality" /><ref name="Fischer" /><ref name="Hayles">{{multiref2|{{Cite book |last=Hayles |first=N. Katherine |title=Immortal Engines: Life Extension and Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |publisher=[[University of Georgia Press]] |year=1996 |isbn=0-8203-1733-0 |editor-last=Slusser |editor-first=George |editor-link=George Edgar Slusser |location=[[Athens, Georgia]] |pages=111–112 |chapter=How Cyberspace Signifies: Taking Immortality Literally |oclc=34319944 |author-link=N. Katherine Hayles |editor-last2=Westfahl |editor-first2=Gary |editor-link2=Gary Westfahl |editor-last3=Rabkin |editor-first3=Eric S.}}|{{Cite book |last=Hayles |first=N. Katherine |title=Bridges to Science Fiction and Fantasy: Outstanding Essays from the J. Lloyd Eaton Conferences |date=2018 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-1-4766-3193-6 |editor-last=Benford |editor-first=Gregory |editor-link=Gregory Benford |pages=151 |language=en |chapter=How Cyberspace Signifies: Taking Immortality Literally |author-link=N. Katherine Hayles |editor-last2=Westfahl |editor-first2=Gary |editor-link2=Gary Westfahl |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dZ1NDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT159}}}}</ref> Attitudes towards this kind of existence vary between and within stories. The argument that it should be no more unappealing than having artificial body parts is made in [[Damien Broderick]]'s 2002 novel ''[[Transcension (novel)|Transcension]]'', while in [[John Crowley (author)|John Crowley]]'s 1979 novel ''[[Engine Summer]]'' it is viewed as a type of imprisonment.<ref name="TheGospelAccordingToScienceFiction">{{Cite book|last=McKee|first=Gabriel|title=The Gospel According to Science Fiction: From The Twilight Zone to the Final Frontier|date=2007|publisher=Westminster John Knox Press|isbn=978-1-61164-426-5|pages=225–226|language=en|chapter=Imagining the Afterlife|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Z11BwAAQBAJ&pg=PA225}}</ref> In Frederik Pohl's 1977–2004 novel series the ''[[Heechee Saga]]'', one character enjoys the capabilities afforded by having vast computational power available directly to the mind, whereas another dreads the prospect of serving the entirety of a millennia-long prison sentence.<ref name="GreenwoodEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="StephenWebbImmortality" /><ref name="TheGospelAccordingToScienceFiction" /> In [[Greg Egan]]'s 2002 novel ''[[Schild's Ladder]]'' the digital existence is so convincing it can be mistaken for the physical world, and Egan's 1994 novel ''[[Permutation City]]'' raises the issue of whether an uploaded mind is the same person or merely a copy.<ref name="GreenwoodEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="Lebow" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Farnell|first=Ross|date=2000|title=Attempting Immortality: AI, A-Life, and the Posthuman in Greg Egan's "Permutation City"|url=https://www.depauw.edu/sfs/backissues/80/farnell80art.htm|journal=[[Science Fiction Studies]]|volume=27|issue=1|pages=69–91|issn=0091-7729|jstor=4240849}}</ref> Another version of the concept is seen in Arthur C. Clarke's ''The City and the Stars'', where the uploaded minds are kept in storage without consciousness for transfer to a new body as one becomes available and then uploaded again when the body dies, allowing for an unlimited number of sequential lifetimes.<ref name="StephenWebbImmortality" />''<ref name="GuthkeClarke" />''

==== Cryonics ====
{{Further|Suspended animation in fiction}}
[[Cryonic freezing]] is used as a means to extend life until such a time that immortality is expected to be available in some stories such as [[Brian Stableford]]'s 1986 short story "[[And He Not Busy Being Born...]]".<ref name="StephenWebbImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /><ref name="SFEncyclopediaCryonics">{{Cite web|last1=Stableford|first1=Brian|author-link=Brian Stableford|last2=Langford|first2=David|author-link2=David Langford|date=2016|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Cryonics|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/cryonics|access-date=2022-02-14|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref> Science fiction writers have generally had a pessimistic outlook on this idea, foreseeing various problems;<ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionCryogenics" /> immortality does not become available within the promised time frame in [[Clifford D. Simak]]'s 1967 novel ''[[Why Call Them Back from Heaven?]]'',<ref name="StephenWebbImmortality" /> everything works as intended but society has changed for the worse in the intervening period in [[Anders Bodelsen]]'s 1969 novel ''[[Freezing Point (Bodelsen novel)|Freezing Point]]'' ({{lang|da|Frysepunktet}}),<ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="SFEncyclopediaCryonics" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Clute|first=John|author-link=John Clute|date=2021|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Bodelsen, Anders|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/bodelsen_anders|access-date=2022-02-18|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref> and the preserved bodies are [[Organ theft|exploited for their organs]] in [[Larry Niven]]'s 1973 short story "[[The Defenseless Dead]]".<ref name="StephenWebbImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionCryogenics">{{Cite book|last=Stableford|first=Brian M.|title=[[Science Fact and Science Fiction: An Encyclopedia]]|date=2006|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-0-415-97460-8|pages=108|language=en|chapter=Cryogenics|author-link=Brian Stableford|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uefwmdROKTAC&pg=PA108}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Pilkington |first=Ace G. |title=Science Fiction and Futurism: Their Terms and Ideas |date=2017 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-0-7864-9856-7 |pages=55 |language=en |chapter=Cryonics |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a2VEDgAAQBAJ&pg=PT67}}</ref>

=== Supernatural and magical ===
The [[Alchemy|alchemical]] substance known as the [[philosopher's stone]] is credited with being able to grant everlasting life in stories such as [[William Godwin]]'s 1799 novel ''[[St. Leon (novel)|St. Leon]]''.<ref name="HorrorImmortal" /><ref name="FantasyEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Clute|first=John|author-link=John Clute|date=1997|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Grant|editor2-first=John|editor2-link=John Grant (author)|title=Godwin, William|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/fe/godwin_william|access-date=2022-01-29|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Fantasy]]|language=en}}</ref> In [[Natalie Babbitt]]'s 1975 novel ''[[Tuck Everlasting (novel)|Tuck Everlasting]]'', a family becomes immortal after drinking from a magical spring.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Clute|first=John|author-link=John Clute|date=1997|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Grant|editor2-first=John|editor2-link=John Grant (author)|title=Babbitt, Natalie|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/fe/babbitt_natalie|access-date=2022-02-19|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Fantasy]]|language=en}}</ref> [[Magician (fantasy)|Magic users]] are often immortal, and magic itself may be the cause of their immortality.<ref name="HorrorImmortal" /><ref>{{multiref2|{{Cite book|last=Jones|first=Diana Wynne|title=[[The Tough Guide to Fantasyland]]|date=2006|isbn=0-14-240722-4|edition=Revised and Updated|location=New York|chapter=Immortals|author-link=Diana Wynne Jones}}|{{Cite book|last=Jones|first=Diana Wynne|title=[[The Tough Guide to Fantasyland]]|date=2006|isbn=0-14-240722-4|edition=Revised and Updated|location=New York|chapter=Magic Users|author-link=Diana Wynne Jones}}}}</ref> The magical [[Land of Oz]] in [[L. Frank Baum]]'s [[Oz series|''Oz'' series]] confers immortality on those living there,<ref name="GreenwoodEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref>{{Cite book|last=Riley|first=Michael O'Neal|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LkBaAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA216|title=Oz and Beyond: The Fantasy World of L. Frank Baum|date=1997|publisher=University Press of Kansas|isbn=978-0-7006-0832-4|pages=216|language=en|chapter=Resolution of Conflict (1917–1919)|quote=The principal problem he addressed was the immortality of the inhabitants, and while repeating what he had said in ''The Emerald City'', that no one died or was sick in Oz but that in rare instances a person could be destroyed, he went on to deal with the American characters: "Another strange thing about this fairy Land of Oz was that whoever managed to enter it from the outside world came under the magic spell of the place and did not change in appearance as long as they lived there."}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Tuerk|first=Richard|title=Oz in Perspective: Magic and Myth in the L. Frank Baum Books|date=2015|publisher=McFarland|isbn=978-0-7864-8291-7|pages=186|language=en|chapter=Boundaries: Oz as Sacred Space|quote=By the twelfth book, nonetheless, the whole Land of Oz constitutes divine space in which mortals from the United States who are lucky enough to get there achieve a kind of immortality.|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ppEFuqS9YsEC&pg=PA186}}</ref> and similarly the towns of Tukwan and Levensvale in Ghanaian author [[Kojo Laing]]'s 1988 [[Magic realism|magical realist]] novel ''[[Woman of the Aeroplanes]]'' are immortal by virtue of existing outside of ordinary time.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cooper |first=Brenda |title=Magical Realism in West African Fiction |date=1998 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=0-203-45139-2 |pages=192 |language=en |chapter=Intermediate Magic and the Fiction of B. Kojo Laing |author-link=<!-- No article at present (May 2022); author of ''To Lay These Secrets Open'' (1992), Associate Professor in the Centre for African Studies at the University of Cape Town --> |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O0H9J_VchLAC&pg=PT189}}</ref><ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Walelign |first=Hiwot |title=The Practice and Significance of Magical Realism in Selected African Novels |date=2020 |publisher=[[Addis Ababa University]] |quote=Levensvale has similar nature and interest with that of Tukwan: it's invisible to United Kingdom and its inhabitants are immortals as well. [...] The invisibility of the town has made the inhabitants out of ordinary time and as a result, they are immortals. |pages=52, 60}}</ref> Immortality is sometimes bestowed upon humans by [[Deity|deities]] (as in the Greek myth of Ganymede) or [[Extraterrestrial intelligence|aliens]] (as in Clifford D. Simak's 1963 novel ''[[Way Station (novel)|Way Station]]''), or received through a [[deal with the Devil]];<ref name="ImmortalityAndLifeExtension" /><ref name="GreenwoodEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="FantasyEncyclopediaImmortality">{{Cite web|last=Stableford|first=Brian|author-link=Brian Stableford|date=1997|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Grant|editor2-first=John|editor2-link=John Grant (author)|title=Immortality|url=http://sf-encyclopedia.uk/fe.php?nm=immortality|access-date=2021-08-21|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Fantasy]]|language=en}}</ref> the title character of [[Oscar Wilde]]'s 1890 novel ''[[The Picture of Dorian Gray]]'' has a portrait that ages in his stead as the result of inadvertently making such a deal.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Guthke |first=Karl Siegfried |title=Life Without End: A Thought Experiment in Literature from Swift to Houellebecq |date=2017 |publisher=Boydell & Brewer |isbn=978-1-57113-974-0 |pages=90–101 |language=en |chapter=The Scandal of Eternal Beauty: Oscar Wilde, ''The Picture of Dorian Gray'' |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cNU1DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA90}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Magnúsdóttir |first=Svanhvít Helga |date=2015 |title=The Battle of Good and Evil in ''The Picture of Dorian Gray'' |url=https://skemman.is/bitstream/1946/22867/1/The%20Battle%20of%20Good%20and%20Evil%20BA.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200321044625/https://skemman.is/bitstream/1946/22867/1/The%20Battle%20of%20Good%20and%20Evil%20BA.pdf |archive-date=2020-03-21 |access-date=2021-08-23 |pages=11–12 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Heise-von der Lippe |first=Anya |title=The Ashgate Encyclopedia of Literary and Cinematic Monsters |date=2014 |publisher=Ashgate Publishing, Ltd. |isbn=978-1-4724-0060-4 |editor-last=Weinstock |editor-first=Jeffrey Andrew |editor-link=Jeffrey Andrew Weinstock |pages=298–301 |language=en |chapter=Gray, Dorian |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Uly8AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA298}}</ref> The legend of the ghost ship the ''[[Flying Dutchman]]'' involves immortality being handed down as divine retribution for the captain's blasphemy. Several stories exist in which universal immortality is caused by the [[personification of Death]] being (temporarily) incapacitated in some way, including [[T. F. Powys]]' 1931 novel ''[[Unclay]]'' and the 1939 film ''[[On Borrowed Time]]''.<ref name="HorrorImmortal">{{Cite book |last=Stableford |first=Brian |title=Icons of Horror and the Supernatural [Two Volumes] |date=2006 |publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group |isbn=978-0-313-08100-2 |editor-last=Joshi |editor-first=S. T. |editor-link=S. T. Joshi |pages=307–340 |language=en |chapter=The Immortal |author-link=Brian Stableford |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CNXZZdER5mQC&pg=PA307}}</ref>

== Outcomes ==
The outcomes of immortality range from a blessing to a curse for the individual, and from utopian to dystopian for society.<ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /><ref name="Botelho" /> Science fiction tends to explore the means by which immortality is attained and occasionally the consequences for individual people, whereas fantasy usually delves more into the enduring societal effects and questions of morality.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Collings |first=Michael R. |title=Death and the Serpent: Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |date=1985 |publisher=Greenwood Press |isbn=0-313-23279-2 |editor-last=Yoke |editor-first=Carl B. |pages=29–30, 36–37 |chapter=The Mechanics of Immortality |oclc=10605246 |author-link=Michael R. Collings |editor-last2=Hassler |editor-first2=Donald M.}}</ref>

=== Negative ===
For the most part, immortality is portrayed as strongly desired yet not truly desirable,<ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Rabkin |first=Eric S. |title=Immortal Engines: Life Extension and Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |publisher=[[University of Georgia Press]] |year=1996 |isbn=0-8203-1733-0 |editor-last=Slusser |editor-first=George |editor-link=George Edgar Slusser |location=[[Athens, Georgia]] |pages=ix–x |chapter=Introduction: Immortality: The ''Self''-Defeating Fantasy |oclc=34319944 |quote=Yet our fictions often tell us that immortality is best only as a hope and never as an actuality, for, despite its venerable, obvious, and intimate appeal, the fantasy of immortality masks a terrible reality. |editor-last2=Westfahl |editor-first2=Gary |editor-link2=Gary Westfahl |editor-last3=Rabkin |editor-first3=Eric S.}}</ref> and the stories it appears in commonly function as a kind of cautionary tale.<ref name="ImmortalityAndLifeExtension" /><ref name="FantasyEncyclopediaImmortality" /> Some stories such as Argentinian author [[Jorge Luis Borges]]' 1947 short story "[[The Immortal (short story)|The Immortal]]" and [[Patrick O'Leary (writer)|Patrick O'Leary]]'s 2002 novel ''[[The Impossible Bird (novel)|The Impossible Bird]]'' go so far as to show immortals seeking to regain their mortality.<ref name="HorrorImmortal" /><ref name="Fischer" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Guthke |first=Karl Siegfried |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cNU1DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA102 |title= Life Without End: A Thought Experiment in Literature from Swift to Houellebecq |date=2017 |publisher=Boydell & Brewer |isbn=978-1-57113-974-0 |pages=102 |language=en |chapter=From God to Caveman: Jorge Luis Borges, "The Immortal"}}</ref> Says [[Brian Stableford]], "When the immortal condition seems perfectly satisfactory in itself, however, the world tends to be found wanting".<ref name="FantasyEncyclopediaImmortality" />

==== Physical and psychological ====
Overwhelming ennui or restlessness is often depicted as an inevitable consequence of everlasting life. [[Satire|Satirical]] treatments of the lengths immortal beings might go to in order to stave off boredom are found in [[Michael Moorcock]]'s 1970s ''[[The Dancers at the End of Time]]'' series and [[Douglas Adams]]' 1982 novel ''[[Life, the Universe and Everything]]''; in the latter, the character [[Wowbagger the Infinitely Prolonged]] spends eternity travelling the universe to insult every living being to their face in alphabetical order.<ref name="StephenWebbImmortality" /><ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /> Another issue faced by immortals in some works is physical deterioration, either due to ongoing natural [[senescence]] or as a direct side-effect of immortality itself, the latter appearing in [[Aldous Huxley]]'s 1939 story ''[[After Many a Summer Dies the Swan]]'' where the immortals slowly transform into ape-like creatures and [[Bob Shaw]]'s 1970 novel ''[[One Million Tomorrows]]'' where immortality causes [[impotence]].<ref name="GreenwoodEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /> While remaining forever childlike in spirit as well as body makes [[J. M. Barrie]]'s [[Peter Pan (character)|Peter Pan]] carefree and joyful, it also leaves him self-centred and unable to form meaningful lasting relationships.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Guthke |first=Karl Siegfried |title=Life Without End: A Thought Experiment in Literature from Swift to Houellebecq |date=2017 |publisher=Boydell & Brewer |isbn=978-1-57113-974-0 |pages=35–42 |language=en |chapter=Euphoria of Eternal Youth: J. M. Barrie, ''Peter Pan'' |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cNU1DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA35}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Lundquist |first=Lynne |title=Immortal Engines: Life Extension and Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |publisher=[[University of Georgia Press]] |year=1996 |isbn=0-8203-1733-0 |editor-last=Slusser |editor-first=George |editor-link=George Edgar Slusser |location=[[Athens, Georgia]] |pages=201–210 |chapter=Living Dolls: Images of Immortality in Children's Literature |oclc=34319944 |editor-last2=Westfahl |editor-first2=Gary |editor-link2=Gary Westfahl |editor-last3=Rabkin |editor-first3=Eric S.}}</ref> On the other hand, the mismatch of having an ageing mind in an eternally youthful body is a cause of distress in multiple stories of child vampires,<ref name="Hauskeller" /> and the 1996 novel ''[[Holy Fire (novel)|Holy Fire]]'' by [[Bruce Sterling]] similarly portrays regaining youth in old age by means of [[rejuvenation]] as having unsettling effects on the psyche.<ref name="Botelho" /> A different psychological side-effect of immortality depicted in some works such as the aforementioned ''In Time,'' the works of [[Roger Zelazny]], and [[Andrei Irkutov]]'s 1924 short story "[[Immortality (Irkutov short story)|Immortality]]" is an ''increased'' fear of death, immortal life being "too precious to risk".<ref name="Hauskeller" /><ref name="Zelazny" /><ref name="Krementsov">{{Cite book |last=Krementsov |first=Nikolai |title=Revolutionary Experiments: The Quest for Immortality in Bolshevik Science and Fiction |date=2013 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-999299-7 |pages=62–63 |language=en |chapter="Professor's Head": Isolated Organs |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EdM8BAAAQBAJ&pg=PA62}}</ref> [[The Nameless One (character)|The Nameless One]], the [[player character]] in the 1999 ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]'' video game ''[[Planescape: Torment]]'', has [[amnesia]] along with immortality; injuries that would have been fatal were it not for his immortality instead cause him to lose consciousness to later awaken without any memories.<ref name="Zaleski" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Jayemanne |first=Darshana |title=Performativity in Art, Literature, and Videogames |date=2017 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-54451-9 |pages=149 |language=en |chapter='A Restless Corpse': Apparatuses, Bodies and Worlds in ''Planescape: Torment'' |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WdksDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA149}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Seijas |first=Casey |date=2011-11-11 |title=Favorite Immortals |url=http://www.ugo.com/movies/best-immortal-characters4658.html?page=2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140519222435/http://www.ugo.com/movies/best-immortal-characters?page=2 |archive-date=2014-05-19 |access-date=2021-12-12 |website=[[UGO Networks]] |language=en}}</ref> Regularly recurring (and thus, functionally, [[Anterograde amnesia|anterograde]]) amnesia is a side-effect of immortality in a different way in [[John R. Pierce]]'s 1944 short story "[[Invariant (short story)|Invariant]]", the consequence of restoring both the body and the mind to a previous state, while one-time (and thus functionally [[Retrograde amnesia|retrograde]]) amnesia is a side-effect of an immortality treatment in [[Christopher Priest (novelist)|Christopher Priest]]'s 1981 novel ''[[The Affirmation]]'',<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Langford|first1=David|author-link=David Langford|last2=Clute|first2=John|author-link2=John Clute|date=2021|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Amnesia|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/amnesia|access-date=2022-02-12|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Langford |first=David |url=https://archive.org/details/sciencefictionwr0000unse |title=Science Fiction Writers: Critical Studies of the Major Authors from the Early Nineteenth Century to the Present Day |date=1999 |publisher=[[Charles Scribner's Sons]] |isbn=0-684-80593-6 |editor-last=Bleiler |editor-first=Richard |editor-link=Richard Bleiler |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=621 |chapter=Christopher Priest |oclc=40460120 |author-link=David Langford}}</ref> and continuous loss of the oldest memories due to the brain's storage capacity being exceeded appears in [[Michael Flynn (writer)|Michael Flynn]]'s 1994 short story "[[Melodies of the Heart]]".<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Ultimate Encyclopedia of Science Fiction: The Definitive Illustrated Guide |date=1996 |publisher=Carlton |isbn=1-85868-188-X |editor-last=Pringle |editor-first=David |editor-link=David Pringle |location= |pages=43 |language=en |chapter=The Elixir of Life |oclc=38373691 |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/ultimateencyclop0000unse_a8c7/page/43/mode/2up}}</ref>

==== Religious ====
In [[Richard Cowper]]'s 1983 short story "[[The Tithonian Factor]]", it is discovered that the [[afterlife]] is real, to the chagrin of those who had already acquired immortality when the discovery was made.<ref name="HorrorImmortal" /><ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /> Similarly, the aforementioned ''Le Grand Secret'' depicts a character having a strong aversion to the prospect of immortality because it would preclude the reincarnation necessary to attain enlightenment according to their [[Hinduism|Hindu]] faith.<ref name="Hendrix" /> Immortality also conflicts with reincarnation in the 1967 short story "[[The Vitanuls]]" by [[John Brunner (novelist)|John Brunner]]; the lack of death results such a shortage of souls that children are eventually born without a soul.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Pfeiffer |first=John R. |url=https://archive.org/details/sciencefictionwr0000unse |title=Science Fiction Writers: Critical Studies of the Major Authors from the Early Nineteenth Century to the Present Day |date=1999 |publisher=[[Charles Scribner's Sons]] |isbn=0-684-80593-6 |editor-last=Bleiler |editor-first=Richard |editor-link=Richard Bleiler |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=126 |chapter=John Brunner |oclc=40460120}}</ref>

==== Social and political ====
In works where immortality is not universal, the immortal ones encounter the drawback of outliving their loved ones, depicted for instance in [[Mary Shelley]]'s 1833 short story "[[The Mortal Immortal]]",<ref name="Zelazny" /><ref name="ClarkHowToLiveForever">{{Cite book|last=Clark|first=Stephen R. L.|title=How to Live Forever: Science Fiction and Philosophy|date=2008|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-134-80007-0|pages=10–13|language=en|chapter=The end of summer|author-link=Stephen R. L. Clark|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1giFAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA10}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gazzaz |first=Rasha Asim Hussein |date=2019 |title=Psychological Anxieties in Mary Shelley's "The Mortal Immortal" |journal=Journal of King Abdulaziz University: Arts and Humanities |volume=27 |issue=5 |pages=249–258 |doi=10.4197/Art.27-5.11 |issn=1658-4295 |doi-access=free}}</ref> whereas fictional societies with universal immortality are inherently susceptible to [[overpopulation]], as seen in ''Le Grand Secret'' and [[Richard Wilson (author)|Richard Wilson]]'s 1965 short story "[[The Eight Billion]]".<ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="Hendrix" /> Authors often couple immortality with infertility to get around the latter problem.<ref name="ImmortalityAndInfertility">{{Cite journal |last1=Grech |first1=Victor E. |last2=Vassallo |first2=Clare |last3=Callus |first3=Ivan |date=2012 |title=Immortality and Infertility in Science Fiction: Who Wants To Live Forever? |url=https://www.um.edu.mt/library/oar/bitstream/123456789/25497/1/immortality%20paper%20sfra%20%282%29.pdf |url-status=live |journal=[[SFRA Review]] |language=en |volume=299 |pages=5–10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210819173102/https://www.um.edu.mt/library/oar/bitstream/123456789/25497/1/immortality%20paper%20sfra%20(2).pdf |archive-date=2021-08-19}}</ref> On the other hand, the absence of reproduction among immortals is also depicted as causing population-wide problems in some works—one example being societal stagnation in [[Algis Budrys]]' 1954 short story ''[[The End of Summer (short story)|The End of Summer]]''—and in [[David H. Keller]]'s 1934 novel ''[[Life Everlasting (Keller novel)|Life Everlasting]]'' the people demand an antidote to restore mortality and fertility both.<ref name="ImmortalityAndInfertility" /><ref name="ClarkHowToLiveForever" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Stableford |first=Brian |url=https://archive.org/details/sciencefictionwr0000unse |title=Science Fiction Writers: Critical Studies of the Major Authors from the Early Nineteenth Century to the Present Day |date=1999 |publisher=[[Charles Scribner's Sons]] |isbn=0-684-80593-6 |editor-last=Bleiler |editor-first=Richard |editor-link=Richard Bleiler |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=399 |chapter=David H. Keller |oclc=40460120 |author-link=Brian Stableford}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Clute |first=John |author-link=John Clute |date=2021 |editor-last=Clute |editor-first=John |editor-link=John Clute |editor2-last=Langford |editor2-first=David |editor2-link=David Langford |editor3-last=Sleight |editor3-first=Graham |editor3-link=Graham Sleight |title=Keller, David H, M D |url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/keller_david_h_m_d |access-date=2022-05-30 |website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref> [[Stephen Southwold|Neil Bell]]'s 1930 novel ''[[The Seventh Bowl]]'' depicts dire societal consequences when immortality drugs are introduced—not due to immortality itself, but rather due to the actions of those in power in response to the new technology as they seek to further their own goals.<ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Stableford|first1=Brian|author-link=Brian Stableford|last2=Clute|first2=John|author-link2=John Clute|date=2020|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Bell, Neil|url=http://www.sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/bell_neil|access-date=2021-08-25|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref> In the 1888 novel ''[[The Inner House (novel)|The Inner House]]'' by [[Walter Besant]], these problems are combined: a life-extending treatment intended to provide additional yet still limited time for a select few instead results in the emergence of an authoritarian society where everyone's life is prolonged indefinitely and strict [[population control]] is enforced where the only births that are allowed are those replacing accidental deaths, resulting in social stagnation in the centuries that follow.<ref name="Botelho">{{Cite book |last=Botelho |first=Teresa |title=Intelligence, Creativity and Fantasy: Proceedings of the 5th International Multidisciplinary Congress (PHI 2019), October 7–9, 2019, Paris, France |publisher=CRC Press |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-000-73406-5 |editor-last=Kong |editor-first=Mário S. Ming |pages=431–436 |language=en |chapter=The cure for death: Fantasies of longevity and immortality in speculative fiction |editor-last2=Monteiro |editor-first2=Maria do Rosário |editor-last3=Neto |editor-first3=Maria João Pereira |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pcO2DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA431}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Stableford|first=Brian|author-link=Brian Stableford|date=2020|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Besant, Walter|url=http://www.sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/besant_walter|access-date=2021-08-29|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref> In [[José Saramago]]'s 2005 novel ''[[Death at Intervals]]'', the unexpected cessation of all death in a society accustomed to its presence causes demographic problems, economic disruption, and shortages of both resources and space.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kundu |first=Devaleena |title=Death Representations in Literature: Forms and Theories |date=2015 |publisher=Cambridge Scholars Publishing |isbn=978-1-4438-7298-0 |editor-last=Teodorescu |editor-first=Adriana |pages=8–23 |language=en |chapter=The Paradox of Mortality: Death and Perpetual Denial |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h_KmBgAAQBAJ&pg=PA8}}</ref> In Moroccan author [[Mohammed Aziz Lahbabi]]'s 1974 novel ''[[The Elixir of Life (novel)|The Elixir of Life]]'', the invention of the titular elixir results in exacerbated [[Social inequality|inequality]], [[class conflict]], and [[social unrest]], in part because the poor are convinced that only the [[Elite|social elite]] will receive the elixir.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Campbell|first=Ian|title=Arabic Science Fiction|date=2018|publisher=Springer International Publishing|isbn=978-3-319-91433-6|location=Cham|pages=82–84|chapter=Criticism and Theory of Arabic SF|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-91433-6_4|author-link=<!-- No article at present (January 2022); author of Fiction and Social Criticism in Morocco of the 1970s: Muḥammad 'Azīz Laḥbābī's ''The Elixir of Life''|url=https://scholarworks.gsu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1038&context=mcl_facpub|url-status=live|journal=[[Science Fiction Studies]]|volume=42|issue=1|pages=42–55|doi=10.5621/sciefictstud.42.1.0042 |issn=0091-7729|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200319010530/https://scholarworks.gsu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1038&context=mcl_facpub|archive-date=2020-03-19|access-date=2022-01-08|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Ahmad|first=Muhammad Aurangzeb|date=2017-06-28|title=Sci-Fi and Speculative Fiction in the Muslim Tradition|url=https://thewire.in/culture/sci-fi-speculative-fiction-muslim-tradition|access-date=2022-01-08|website=[[The Wire (India)|The Wire]]}}</ref> In Egyptian author [[Tawfiq al-Hakim]]'s 1947 short story "[[In the Year One Million]]", a future society that has eliminated death and disease is also devoid of love and the arts, leading the populace to rise up to reverse these developments in order to regain meaning; al-Hakim's 1958 play ''[[Voyage to Tomorrow]]'' was based on the short story and expands on its themes.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Campbell|first=Ian|title=Arabic Science Fiction|date=2018|publisher=Springer International Publishing|isbn=978-3-319-91433-6|location=Cham|pages=71|chapter=Arabic SF: Definitions and Origins|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-91433-6_3|author-link=<!-- |last=Determann |first=Jörg Matthias |title=Islam, Science Fiction and Extraterrestrial Life: The Culture of Astrobiology in the Muslim World |date=2020 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=978-0-7556-0129-5 |pages=85 |language=en |chapter=Trips to the Moon |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=k1_xDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA85}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bould |first=Mark |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170412061255/https://sfra.org/resources/sfra-review/311.pdf |archive-date=2017-04-12}}</ref>

==== Moral ====
In works of horror, the cost of immortality is typically the loss of one's humanity.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Vasbinder |first=Samuel H. |title=Death and the Serpent: Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |date=1985 |publisher=Greenwood Press |isbn=0-313-23279-2 |editor-last=Yoke |editor-first=Carl B. |pages=71–72 |chapter=Deathless Humans in Horror Fiction |oclc=10605246 |editor-last2=Hassler |editor-first2=Donald M.}}</ref> The moral cost of attaining immortality is viewed as unacceptable in some works where it hinges on the deaths of others.<ref name="Hauskeller" /> In Larry Niven's 1967 short story "[[The Jigsaw Man]]", immortality is achieved by [[Organ transplantation|organ transplants]], but there is a chronic shortage of organs. For this reason, [[Organ harvesting|organs are harvested]] from executed criminals, which leads to use of the death penalty being expanded to include a wider variety of crimes to meet the demand, eventually including [[traffic violation]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dooley |first=Linda Rinker |title=Death and the Serpent: Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |date=1985 |publisher=Greenwood Press |isbn=0-313-23279-2 |editor-last=Yoke |editor-first=Carl B. |pages=157–158 |chapter=Larry Niven: Immortality and Unstable Equilibrium |oclc=10605246 |editor-last2=Hassler |editor-first2=Donald M.}}</ref>

==== Alienation ====
[[Social alienation|Alienation]] is a common consequence of immortality.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Rosen|first=S. L.|title=Immortal Engines: Life Extension and Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy|publisher=[[University of Georgia Press]]|year=1996|isbn=0-8203-1733-0|editor-last=Slusser|editor-first=George|editor-link=George Edgar Slusser|location=[[Athens, Georgia]]|pages=125–134|chapter=Alienation as the Price of Immortality: The Tithonus Syndrome in Science Fiction and Fantasy|oclc=34319944|editor-last2=Westfahl|editor-first2=Gary|editor-link2=Gary Westfahl|editor-last3=Rabkin|editor-first3=Eric S.}}</ref> Immortals in otherwise mortal societies often feel the need to hide their immortality lest they be locked up in a laboratory for study. This problem is faced by the immortal group of people in the aforementioned ''The Immortals'' by James Gunn as well as in the 1970 television series ''[[The Immortal (1970 TV series)|The Immortal]]'' inspired by Gunn's novel. The lone immortal title characters in the aforementioned ''The Man from Earth'' and the 2015 film ''[[The Age of Adaline]]'' additionally experience the loneliness of having to uproot their lives and move every ten years or so to keep the people around them from noticing that they do not age.<ref name="GreenwoodEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="TheManFromEarth" /><ref name="TheAgeOfAdaline">{{Cite web |last=Westfahl |first=Gary |author-link=Gary Westfahl |date=2015-04-25 |title=Methuselah's Daughter: A Review of The Age of Adaline |url=https://locusmag.com/2015/04/methuselahs-daughter-a-review-of-the-age-of-adaline/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210825050726/https://locusmag.com/2015/04/methuselahs-daughter-a-review-of-the-age-of-adaline/ |archive-date=2021-08-25 |access-date=2021-08-25 |website=[[Locus Online]] |language=en-US}}</ref> In the 1974 novella "[[Born with the Dead]]" by [[Robert Silverberg]], immortality is attained by being [[Resurrection|resurrected]] after death, and those that have gone through that procedure become estranged from the rest of society due to the emotional effects.<ref name="AgeingAndImmortality">{{Cite book |last=Stableford |first=Brian |title=[[The Science in Science Fiction]] |date=1983 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-53010-1 |editor-last=Nicholls |editor-first=Peter |editor-link=Peter Nicholls (writer) |location=New York |pages=144–146 |chapter=Ageing and immortality |oclc=8689657 |author-link=Brian Stableford |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/scienceinscience00nich/page/144/mode/2up}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Stableford|first1=Brian|author-link=Brian Stableford|last2=Clute|first2=John|author-link2=John Clute|date=2021|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Silverberg, Robert|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/silverberg_robert|access-date=2021-12-12|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Edwards |first=Malcolm |url=https://archive.org/details/sciencefictionwr0000unse |title=Science Fiction Writers: Critical Studies of the Major Authors from the Early Nineteenth Century to the Present Day |date=1999 |publisher=[[Charles Scribner's Sons]] |isbn=0-684-80593-6 |editor-last=Bleiler |editor-first=Richard |editor-link=Richard Bleiler |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=710 |chapter=Robert Silverberg |oclc=40460120 |author-link=Malcolm Edwards}}</ref>

=== Positive ===
There are also works with enthusiastic or outright [[Utopian fiction|utopian]] visions of immortality, such as the 1928 novel ''[[My First Two Thousand Years]]'' by [[Paul Eldridge]] and [[George Sylvester Viereck]] which portrays the life of a lone immortal as being a position of privilege. In these positive depictions, immortality is typically not universal. A notable exception is [[George Bernard Shaw]]'s 1921 story ''[[Back to Methuselah]]'', which was repudiated by [[Karel Čapek]] who included a counterargument in the preface to his 1925 play ''[[The Makropulos Secret|The Makropoulos Secret]]''.<ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Blackford |first=Russell |title=Science Fiction and the Moral Imagination: Visions, Minds, Ethics |date=2017 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-61685-8 |pages=167–170 |language=en |chapter=Imagining Immortality |series=Science and Fiction |author-link=Russell Blackford |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jlU0DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA167}}</ref> [[Eden Phillpotts]]' 1916 story ''[[The Girl and the Faun]]'' takes the position that the costs of immortality are outweighed by its benefits.<ref name="FantasyEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="AToZFantasyImmortality">{{Cite book |last=Stableford |first=Brian |title=The A to Z of Fantasy Literature |date=2009 |publisher=Scarecrow Press |isbn=978-0-8108-6345-3 |pages=214–216 |language=en |chapter=Immortality |quote=The suggestion that boredom, alienation, and the continual loss of loved ones might be prices well worth paying for the reward of eternal life is relatively rare, although it is acknowledged in Eden Phillpotts's ''The Girl and the Faun'' and loudly trumpeted by George Bernard Shaw's ''Back to Methuselah'' (1921) and by George S. Viereck and Paul Eldridge in ''My First Two Thousand Years''. |author-link=Brian Stableford |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7JKw5FYA4GgC&pg=PA215}}</ref>

Soviet author Andrei Irkutov envisioned the advent of a [[proletarian revolution]] as a result of an immortality treatment being invented in his 1924 short story "Immortality". In the story, immortality is granted to those in power and their enforcers, whereas the workers have no interest in it as they do not wish to carry on their labour forever. Consequently, the immortals dare not fight back against the revolution for fear of losing their immortal lives.<ref name="Krementsov" />

In [[feminist science fiction]], immortality presents an opportunity for women to overcome the constraints imposed on them by [[Patriarchy#Feminist theory|patriarchal structures]]. In the 1978 novel ''[[Up the Walls of the World]]'' by Alice Sheldon (pen name [[James Tiptree Jr.]]), an immortal [[cyborg]] uses her powers to promote feminist values. [[Octavia E. Butler]]'s 1980 novel ''[[Wild Seed (novel)|Wild Seed]]'' contrasts the different forms of immortality of its two immortal characters representing masculinity and femininity, respectively; the former relies on killing other people and taking over their bodies whereas the latter is a regenerative kind of immortality which can be used to help others. In both ''Up the Walls of the World'' and ''Wild Seed'', immortality is portrayed as desirable provided that it is combined with love and togetherness.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Roberts |first=Robin |title=Immortal Engines: Life Extension and Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |publisher=[[University of Georgia Press]] |year=1996 |isbn=0-8203-1733-0 |editor-last=Slusser |editor-first=George |editor-link=George Edgar Slusser |location=[[Athens, Georgia]] |pages=135–144 |chapter="No Woman Born": Immortality and Gender in Feminist Science Fiction |oclc=34319944 |author-link=<!-- No article at present (November 2021); author of ''A New Species: Gender and Science in Science Fiction'' (1993), associate professor of English at Louisiana State University, and seems to have been born in 1957 --> |editor-last2=Westfahl |editor-first2=Gary |editor-link2=Gary Westfahl |editor-last3=Rabkin |editor-first3=Eric S.}}</ref>

=== Other ===
Other works take a more dispassionate and analytical view of immortality.<ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /> The immortal life of ''The Man from Earth'' is portrayed as neither a curse nor a blessing, in contrast to writer [[Jerome Bixby]]'s previous work on immortality—the 1969 ''[[Star Trek: The Original Series|Star Trek]]'' episode "[[Requiem for Methuselah]]".<ref name="ImmortalityAndLifeExtension" /><ref name="TheManFromEarth" /> [[Robert Reed]]'s 2004 [[alternate history]] work ''[[A Plague of Life]]'' examines the consequences of universal immortality on human evolution.<ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /> [[Kate Wilhelm]]'s 1983 novel ''[[Welcome, Chaos]]'' depicts the effects of immortality on the then-ongoing [[Cold War]].<ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Langford|first=David|author-link=David Langford|date=2020|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Cold War|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/cold_war|access-date=2022-02-14|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref> Poul Anderson's 1989 novel ''[[The Boat of a Million Years]]'' posits that rather than immortals being stagnant and mortals changing, both can be either.<ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Miesel |first=Sandra |url=https://archive.org/details/sciencefictionwr0000unse |title=Science Fiction Writers: Critical Studies of the Major Authors from the Early Nineteenth Century to the Present Day |date=1999 |publisher=[[Charles Scribner's Sons]] |isbn=0-684-80593-6 |editor-last=Bleiler |editor-first=Richard |editor-link=Richard Bleiler |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=20 |chapter=Poul Anderson |oclc=40460120 |author-link=Sandra Miesel}}</ref>

While there are a large number of stories where immortality enables the unscrupulous to consolidate power, the 1954 novel ''[[They'd Rather Be Right]]'' ({{Aka}} ''The Forever Machine'') by [[Mark Clifton]] and [[Frank Riley (author)|Frank Riley]] envisions a scenario where that cannot happen. In the story, there is a computer which can confer immortality on individuals. In doing so, it also alters their minds in a way that removes negative qualities and preconceived notions. The end result is that most people turn it down because they are not willing to give up their prejudices.<ref name="AgeingAndImmortality" /><ref>{{multiref2|{{Cite web |last=Langford |first=David |author-link=David Langford |date=1982 |title=They'd Rather Be Right |url=https://ansible.uk/writing/ratherbe.html |access-date=2021-12-12 |website=[[Ansible (magazine)|Ansible]]}}|{{Cite web |last=Langford |first=David |author-link=David Langford |date=2008 |title=Rotten Apple |url=https://ansible.uk/sfx/sfx168.html |access-date=2021-12-12 |website=[[Ansible (magazine)|Ansible]]}}}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Clute|first1=John|author-link=John Clute|last2=Langford|first2=David|author-link2=David Langford|date=2021|editor-last=Clute|editor-first=John|editor-link=John Clute|editor2-last=Langford|editor2-first=David|editor2-link=David Langford|editor3-last=Sleight|editor3-first=Graham|editor3-link=Graham Sleight|title=Clifton, Mark|url=https://sf-encyclopedia.com/entry/clifton_mark|access-date=2021-12-12|website=[[The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]]}}</ref>

[[Jack Vance]]'s 1956 novel ''[[To Live Forever (novel)|To Live Forever]]'' reflects the author's belief that immortality is not inherently either good or bad, but rather that it depends on the surrounding circumstances. In the novel, immortality is only granted to those who have made the greatest contributions to society in order to avoid overpopulation. As a result, citizens spend their lives struggling to prove themselves worthy of this reward, and those who have received it subsequently lead cautious lives so as not to risk losing their hard-earned deathlessness to violence or accidents. An alternative to the constraints of this society is proposed within the story: using immortality to explore the cosmos.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Shreve |first=Gregory M. |title=Death and the Serpent: Immortality in Science Fiction and Fantasy |date=1985 |publisher=Greenwood Press |isbn=0-313-23279-2 |editor-last=Yoke |editor-first=Carl B. |pages=185–191 |chapter=The Jaded Eternals: Immortality and Imperfection in Jack Vance's ''To Live Forever'' |oclc=10605246 |editor-last2=Hassler |editor-first2=Donald M.}}</ref>

With regard to the effect of immortality on one's personality, a couple of works have been suggested to demonstrate immortals being enabled to develop their masculine and feminine sides alike,<ref name="TheAgeOfAdaline" /> and in contrast to the more common depiction of immortals as overcome with ennui, the works of Roger Zelazny portray them as insatiably curious. Zelazny likewise eschews the notion that stagnation is an inevitability for immortals, taking the opposite view that previous experiences enhance future ones and that there is consequently always more to learn and experience in order to grow as a person.<ref name="SFEncyclopediaImmortality" /><ref name="ScienceFactAndScienceFictionLongevity" /><ref name="Zelazny">{{Cite journal |last=Francavilla |first=Joseph V. |date=1984 |title=These Immortals: An Alternative View of Immortality in Roger Zelazny's Science Fiction |journal=[[Extrapolation (journal)|Extrapolation]] |language=en |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=20–33 |doi=10.3828/extr.1984.25.1.20 |issn=0014-5483}}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Latin American Gothic
======================================================================

{{Short description|Gothic fiction genre}}
[[File: Juan Manuel Blanes Episodio de la Fiebre Amarilla.jpg|thumb|[[Juan Manuel Blanes]], ''An episode of Yellow Fever in Buenos Aires'' (1871), oil on canvas, [[National Museum of Visual Arts (Uruguay)|National Museum of Visual Arts]] (Uruguay).]]
'''Latin American Gothic''' is a subgenre of [[Gothic fiction]] that draws on Gothic themes and aesthetics and adapts them to the political and geographical specificities of [[Latin America]]. While its origins can be traced back to 20th century [[Latin American literature]] and [[Latin American cinema|cinema]], it was in the first decades of the 21st century that it gained particular relevance as a literary current.

== Characteristics ==
If Gothic fiction, in general, is characterized by an appeal to negative emotional responses triggered by confrontation with [[alterity]], the narrative [[transculturation]] exercised in its Latin American variety doubles the stakes by rendering both foreign and local elements alien.<ref name=":2" /> Themes such as the threat of the [[supernatural]], the intrusion of the past into the present, the blurred line between [[science]] and [[religion]], or the repression of [[Human sexuality|sexuality]] serve to unveil the spectres that haunt Latin America's historical past and current political situation in order to explore the sources of fear and unease in its different countries and regions. In this way, the resources of Gothic fiction make it possible to address issues such as the [[genocide of Indigenous peoples]], [[Class conflict|class struggle]], [[enforced disappearance]]s, and [[Sexist violence|patriarchal violence]].

== Origins ==
Despite being sometimes portrayed as a ruptural phenomenon, the emergence of Gothic themes and topics in 21st century Latin American literature can also be regarded as a variation on a regional literary tradition woven into [[magic realism]] and the [[Fantasy literature|fantastic]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=Latin American gothic in literature and culture |date=2017 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-23422-2 |editor-last=Casanova-Vizcaíno |editor-first=Sandra |series=Routledge interdisciplinary perspectives on literature |location=New York |editor-last2=Ordiz |editor-first2=Inés}}</ref> Literary scholar Soledad Quereilhac argues that the circulation of European Gothic works in nineteenth-century [[Argentina]], along with the proliferation of [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscientific]] and [[occult]] themes in the popular press, led to a local renewal of the genre, as witnessed by the work of authors such as [[Leopoldo Lugones]], [[Eduardo Wilde]], [[Eduardo Ladislao Holmberg|Eduardo Holmberg]] and, most notably, [[Horacio Quiroga]].<ref name=":0" /> The novel ''[[The Shrouded Woman]]'' (1938), by [[Chile]]an writer [[María Luisa Bombal]], has been often singled out as one of the most direct antecedents of contemporary Latin American Gothic fiction.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Raíces y desinencias del nuevo gótico latinoamericano |url=https://www.elsaltodiario.com/literatura/raices-y-desinencias-del-nuevo-gotico-latinoamericano |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=www.elsaltodiario.com |language=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Gótico latinoamericano |url=https://www.lavanguardia.com/cultura/20211016/7789624/gotico-latinoamericano.html |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=www.lavanguardia.com}}</ref> Bombal's novel, narrated first-person by a dead woman in her coffin and touching on themes such as [[abortion]] and issues of power and submission, was a major influence on [[Juan Rulfo]]'s ''[[Pedro Páramo]]'' (1955), which, in addition to being a precursor of magic realism, can also be credited with having helped to pave the way for the regional development of the Gothic.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Miramontes |first=Ana |date=2004 |title=Rulfo lector de Bombal |url=https://www.literatura.us/maria/ana.pdf |journal=Revista iberoamericana |volume=LXX |issue=207 |pages=491–520}}</ref> In the second half of the 20th century, some remarkable forerunners of this literary subgenre include the macabre and darkly erotic short stories by [[Uruguay]]an writer [[Armonía Somers]] (pub. 1950–1994) and the [[haunted house]] themed novella ''La mansión de Araucaima'' (1973), which [[Colombia]]n author [[Álvaro Mutis]] wrote following a debate with [[Spain|Spanish]]-[[Mexico|Mexican]] filmmaker [[Luis Buñuel]] over the possibility of transposing the themes of English Gothic fiction to a tropical setting.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Eljaiek Rodríguez |first=Gabriel Andrés |title=Selva de fantasmas: el gótico en la literatura y el cine latinoamericanos |date=2017 |publisher=Pontificia Universidad Javeriana |isbn=978-958-781-086-8 |edition=Primera edición |series=Ópera eximia |location=Bogotá}}</ref>

== Gothic Literature in Mexico ==
[[File:Rulfo por Lyon.jpg|thumb|Juan Rulfo, a Mexican writer, screenwriter, and photographer. He is best known for two literary works, the novel [[Pedro Páramo|''Pedro'' ''Páramo'']] (1955), and the collection of short stories ''[[El Llano en llamas]]'' (1953).]]
Gothic Literature was introduced in Mexico during the 19th century as a result of [[Romanticism|European Romanticism]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Shelton |first=Laura |chapter=Romanticism in Mexico |title=The Oxford Handbook of Mexican History |pages=0 |editor-last=Beezley |editor-first=William |chapter-url=https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/34726/chapter-abstract/296490839?redirectedFrom=fulltext |access-date=2025-03-11 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-069919-2}}</ref> It was during this time that Mexico's [[Mexican War of Independence|War of Independence]] (1810–1821) shifted political and cultural views, giving rise to literary movements that sought to explore difficult themes ranging from identity to historical colonial trauma.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mexican literature: Writers, genres, and books |url=https://mexicanroutes.com/mexican-literature-writers-genres-and-books/ |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=mexicanroutes.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

Some of the few authors who derived influence from the genre were [[Ignacio Manuel Altamirano]] and [[Manuel Payno]]''.''<ref>{{Citation |title=Ignacio Manuel Altamirano |date=2025-01-21 |work=Wikipedia |url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignacio_Manuel_Altamirano |access-date=2025-03-11 |language=en}}</ref> They adapted Gothic elements to Mexican settings and used them to critique political turmoil of the time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Roura |first=Sergio |title=Asomos góticos en la narrativa breve de Manuel Payno |url=https://www.academia.edu/95865749/Asomos_g%C3%B3ticos_en_la_narrativa_breve_de_Manuel_Payno |journal=Tropelías: Revista de Teoría de la Literatura y Literatura Comparada}}</ref> Altamirano's most notable work ''[[:es:El Zarco|El Zarco]]'' (1901) incorporated those same levels of suspense as found in the common Gothic novel. It emphasized the struggle of the rural working class in a society facing historical colonial trauma, by using bandits that fought among the ranks of [[Benito Juárez]], a Mexican military commander.

Payno's novel ''[[:es:Los bandidos de Río Frío (novela)|Los bandidos de Río Frío]]'' (1891) also uses the idea of the bandit to tell the story of the corruption experienced in post-independence Mexico. It was through this that many 20th century authors such as [[Juan Rulfo]] were able to hone in on Gothic themes present in the aforementioned authors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kadir |first=Djelal |date=1976-01-01 |title=Same Voices, Other Tombs: Structures of Mexican Gothic |url=https://newprairiepress.org/sttcl/vol1/iss1/4 |journal=Studies in 20th & 21st Century Literature |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |doi=10.4148/2334-4415.1032 |issn=2334-4415|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Rulfo's most famous work [[Pedro Páramo]] (1955) sought inspiration from [[María Luisa Bombal]]'s ''[[The Shrouded Woman]]'' (1938), a novel describing the experiences of Ana María, a recently deceased woman as she is prepared for burial.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Velasquez |first=Yader |title=Las innovaciones en La Amortajada, obra de María Luisa Bombal. |url=https://alastorliterario.com/articulo/las-innovaciones-en-la-amortajada-obra-de-maria-lu/ |access-date=2025-03-11 |website=alastorliterario.com |language=en}}</ref> Rulfo builds upon Bombal's exploration of death in the fictitious, barren town of Comala. The town's desolation mirrored not only personal and familial tragedies but also Mexico's post-revolutionary struggles. In this way, Gothic literature intertwined with Mexican history to cunningly shape a distinctive perspective within the genre.<ref>{{Cite web |last=González |first=Keri |title=Memorias entrecruzadas: La amortajada y Pedro Páramo |url=https://www.literatura.us/maria/keri.pdf |website=www.literatura.us}}</ref>

== Contemporary figures ==
[[File:Mariana Enríquez en la Feria Internacional del Libro de Buenos Aires.jpg|thumb|Mariana Enríquez at the [[Buenos Aires International Book Fair]] (2022).]]
The modern Latin American literary Gothic stands out for its predominantly female protagonism. Examples include [[Mariana Enríquez]], an Argentine writer whose works feature disturbed women, sinister children, and eerie physical environments and deal with themes such as the legacy of [[military dictatorship]]s, the emotional consequences of [[exile]], [[femicide]], and [[Police brutality|police violence]]. She achieved international recognition after the publication of her second book of short stories, ''[[Things We Lost in the Fire (story collection)|Things We Lost in the Fire]]'' (2016), which became a bestseller and was translated into more than a dozen languages. She later won the [[Premio Herralde|Herralde Novel Prize]] for ''Our Share of Night'' (2019) and was shortlisted for the 2021 [[International Booker Prize]] for [[Megan McDowell]]'s English translation of her first book of short stories, ''[[The Dangers of Smoking in Bed]]'' (2009).<ref>{{Cite journal |last= Fernández |first=Silvia Beatriz |date=2022-11-29 |title=El terror gótico latinoamericano de Mariana Enriquez como propuesta virtual en el museo Malba: una crítica social y de género |url=http://journals.openedition.org/alhim/11238 |journal=Amérique Latine Histoire et Mémoire |issue=44 |doi=10.4000/alhim.11238 |issn=1628-6731|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-10-07 |title="No quiero que me saquen las pesadillas" {{!}} Babelia {{!}} EL PAÍS |url=https://elpais.com/cultura/2016/04/27/babelia/1461752532_057036.html |access-date=2024-03-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171007152600/https://elpais.com/cultura/2016/04/27/babelia/1461752532_057036.html |archive-date=2017-10-07 }}</ref>

[[Ecuador]]ian writer [[Mónica Ojeda]] rose to prominence thanks to the critical acclaim she received for her third novel ''Jawbone'' (2018), which follows the story of a horror-obsessed teenage girl who is kidnapped by her literature teacher and was shortlisted, in translation by [[Sarah Booker]], for the 2022 [[National Book Award for Translated Literature|National Book Award]]. Ojeda's 2020 short story collection ''[[Las voladoras]]''—which includes ''[[Caninos (short story)|Caninos]]'', previously published in 2017—explores themes such as [[Gender-related violence|gender violence]], abortion, incest, child abuse, sexuality, and religion through the lens of what she defines as "Andean Gothic". It earned Ojeda further critical acclaim and was shortlisted for the [[Premio de Narrativa Breve Ribera del Duero|Ribera del Duero]] literary award.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Marcos |first=Javier Rodríguez |date=2018-05-30 |title=¿Quién demonios es Mónica Ojeda? |url=https://elpais.com/cultura/2018/05/29/actualidad/1527607645_152643.html |access-date=2024-03-13 |work=El País |language=es |issn=1134-6582}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-02-19 |title=El Telégrafo - Noticias del Ecuador y del mundo - Ojeda, Baudoin y Erlés entre finalistas del Premio Ribera del Duero |url=https://www.eltelegrafo.com.ec/noticias/cultura/10/finalistas-riberadel-duero |access-date=2024-03-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200219140937/https://www.eltelegrafo.com.ec/noticias/cultura/10/finalistas-riberadel-duero |archive-date=2020-02-19 }}</ref>

[[Giovanna Rivero]] is one of the most successful contemporary writers in her native [[Bolivia]]. Her work has begun to gain international recognition since the publication of her book of short stories ''Fresh Dirt from the Grave'' (2021), which moves between [[Horror fiction|horror]] and [[science fiction]] and expands the boundaries of the Gothic to engage with [[Pre-Columbian era|pre-Columbian]] ritual and folk tales.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fresh Dirt from the Grave |url=https://charcopress.com/bookstore/fresh-dirt-from-the-grave |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=Charco Press |language=en-GB}}</ref>

[[Michelle Roche Rodríguez]]'s novel ''Malasangre'', about a young girl from a [[Catholic Church|Catholic]] and conservative family who becomes a blood-sucking monster in 1920s [[Caracas]], was shortlisted for the 2021 [[Premio Celsius|Celsius]] literary award, which recognises the best works of science fiction, fantasy, and horror written in [[Spanish language|Spanish]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Literatura |first=Cine y |date=2020-07-08 |title="Malasangre": La novela revelación de la nueva literatura venezolana |url=https://www.cineyliteratura.cl/malasangre-la-novela-revelacion-de-la-nueva-literatura-venezolana/ |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=Cine y Literatura |language=es}}</ref> Roche Rodríguez has been compared to her countryman [[Juan Carlos Chirinos]], who also makes use of Gothic aesthetics to portray the social reality of [[Venezuela]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-03-20 |title=Una historia de vampiros en Venezuela |url=https://www.abc.es/cultura/cultural/abci-historia-vampiros-venezuela-202003200135_noticia.html |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=Diario ABC |language=es}}</ref>

Other authors sometimes classed within the Latin American Gothic movement are [[María Fernanda Ampuero]], [[Fernanda Melchor]], and [[Samanta Schweblin]].

== Film and television ==
[[File:Carlos mayolo.jpg|thumb|The Colombian filmmaker Carlos Mayolo defined his aesthetics as "Tropical Gothic".]]
In the 1980s, [[Colombia]]n filmmakers [[Carlos Mayolo]] and [[Luis Ospina]], members of the so-called "Cali group" or "Caliwood", coined the expression "Tropical Gothic" to refer to the aesthetics of their films, which feature monstrous narratives set against a backdrop of sunlight, warm climates, and an abundance of natural resources.<ref name=":1">{{Citation |last=Ajuria Ibarra |first=Enrique |chapter=Latin American Gothic |date=2022-03-24 |title=Twenty-First-Century Gothic |pages=263–275 |chapter-url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9781474440943-020/html |access-date=2024-03-14 |publisher=Edinburgh University Press |language=en |doi=10.1515/9781474440943-020 |isbn=978-1-4744-4094-3|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> According to scholars Justin D. Edwards and Sandra Guardini Vasconcelos, the [[Tropics]] are fertile ground for the Gothic due to its history of violence and transculturation that involves both the myths that were brought to the region by the European settlers and haunt it under the guise of its colonial past, and an older belief system that is constantly in the process of being unearthed, acknowledged, and remembered in awe and wonder.<ref name=":1" /> Mayolo directed the films ''[[Bloody Flesh]]'' (1983), a tale of incest and cannibalistic undead creatures set during the military dictatorship of [[Gustavo Rojas Pinilla]], and ''[[La Mansión de Araucaima|La mansión de Araucaima]]'' (1986), based on the ''novella'' by Álvaro Mutis about a mysterious house that keeps a group of people trapped by their own fears and repressed desires. Luis Ospina was the director of [[Pura sangre (film)|''Pura Sangre'']] (1982), which is one of the first Colombian [[vampire]] films and which, like ''Bloody Flesh'', uses vampirism as an allegory of the bleeding of the working classes of the [[Valle del Cauca Department|Cauca Valley]] by the local businessmen.

Among more recent films, ''[[La Llorona (2019 film)|La Llorona]]'' (2019), by [[Guatemala]]n filmmaker [[Jayro Bustamante]], places the [[Mesoamerica]]n [[ghost]] legend of [[La Llorona]] in the context of the 1981-1983 [[Guatemalan genocide|Mayan genocide]]. The film was nominated for the [[Golden Globe Awards|Golden Globe]], [[Goya Awards|Goya]], and [[Ariel Award|Ariel]] awards and won the Director's Award at the [[Giornate degli Autori]] of the [[Venice Film Festival]].

Also critically acclaimed was [[Pablo Larraín]]'s [[black comedy]] ''[[El Conde (film)|El Conde]]'' (2023), in which Chilean dictator [[Augusto Pinochet]] is portrayed as a two hundred and fifty year old vampire. It received an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nomination for Best Cinematography and was nominated to the [[Golden Lion]] and winner for Best Screenplay at the Venice Film Festival.

On television, the [[miniseries]] [[Santa Evita (TV series)|''Santa Evita'']] (2022), inspired by the [[Santa Evita|novel of the same name]] by [[Tomás Eloy Martínez]] (1995), offers a fictionalised account of the fate of the embalmed corpse of [[Eva Perón]] framed in a phantasmagorical atmosphere and bordering on the supernatural.

== Other media ==

The style of Argentine visual artist [[Santiago Caruso]], who illustrated the covers of many works of Gothic, horror, and fantasy fiction, ranging from [[Alejandra Pizarnik]]'s ''The Bloody Countess'' to the [[Comte de Lautréamont]]'s ''[[Les Chants de Maldoror]]'', has often been described as Gothic.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=David |date=2014-10-06 |title=Interview: Santiago Caruso {{!}} David Davis |url=https://weirdfictionreview.com/2014/10/interview-santiago-caruso/ |access-date=2024-03-14 |website=Weird Fiction Review |language=en-US}}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Latin American literature
