== Sales and profits ==
The numbers of [[:Category:21st-century short story writers|21st-century short story writers]] run into the thousands.{{Citation needed|date=August 2021}} Female short story writers have gained increased critical attention, with British authors, in particular, exploring modern feminist politics in their writings.{{sfn|Young|2018|p=1}}

Sales of short-story fiction are strong. In the UK, sales jumped 45% in 2017, driven by collections from international names such as Alice Munro, a high number of new writers to the genre, including famous names like actor [[Tom Hanks]] (plus those who publish their work using readily accessible, digital tools), and the revival of short story [[Salon (gathering)|salons]] such as those held by the short fiction company Pin Drop Studio.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sales of short story collections surge {{!}} The Bookseller |url=https://www.thebookseller.com/news/short-story-collections-surge-half-value-and-third-volume-2017-709376 |access-date=2018-04-17 |website=www.thebookseller.com |language=en}}</ref>

More than 690,000 short stories and [[anthologies]] were sold in the UK in 2017, generating £5.88 million, the genre's highest sales since 2010.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Moore |first=Matthew |date=27 January 2018 |title=Short story revival cuts novels down to size |language=en |work=The Times |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/short-story-revival-cuts-novels-down-to-size-mj6xzz535 |issn=0140-0460}}</ref> Throughout the 2010s, there was frequent speculation about a potential "renaissance"; [[Sam Baker (writer)|Sam Baker]] called it a "perfect literary form for the 21st century".{{sfn|Young|2018|p=2}}

Canadian short story writers include [[Alice Munro]], [[Mavis Gallant]] and Lynn Coady. In 2013, Alice Munro became the first writer of nothing but short stories to be awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Literature]]. Her award-winning short story collections include ''[[Dance of the Happy Shades]], [[Lives of Girls and Women]], [[Who Do You Think You Are? (book)|Who Do You Think You Are?]], [[The Progress of Love]], [[The Love of a Good Woman]]'' and ''[[Runaway (book)|Runaway]]''.

== Awards ==
Prominent short story awards such as the [[Sunday Times Short Story Award]], the [[BBC National Short Story Award]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/articles/2QXsYTZYWZ40CTc8lbH0FdV/how-to-enter |title=The BBC National Short Story Award 2020 with Cambridge University |publisher=BBC Radio 4 |access-date=24 August 2021 }}</ref> the Royal Society of Literature's V.S. Pritchett Short Story Prize,<ref>{{cite web| url = https://rsliterature.org/award/v-s-pritchett-short-story-prize/| title = V. S. Pritchett Short Story Prize – Royal Society of Literature| date = 8 November 2017}}</ref> The London Magazine Short Story Prize,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The London Magazine Short Story Prize 2019 |url=https://www.thelondonmagazine.org/the-london-magazine-short-story-prize-2019/ |website=www.thelondonmagazine.org|date=6 November 2019 }}</ref> the Pin Drop Studio Short Story Award and many others attract hundreds of entries each year. Published and non-published writers take part, sending in their stories from around the world.<ref name="PinDrop">{{Cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/10831961/The-irresistible-rise-of-the-short-story.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220111/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/10831961/The-irresistible-rise-of-the-short-story.html |archive-date=2022-01-11 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=The irresistible rise of the short story. Pin Drop Studio|last=Baker|first=Sam|work=Daily Telegraph|date=2014-05-18|access-date=2018-03-21|language=en-GB|issn=0307-1235}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url= https://www.thebookseller.com/news/fuller-wins-royal-academy-pin-drop-short-story-prize-338201 |title=Fuller wins annual Royal Academy & Pin Drop short story prize |website = The Bookseller |last=Onwuemezi|first=Natasha |date=June 27, 2016|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://shortstoryaward.co.uk/articles/view/97 |title=The top short story competitions to enter |work = The Sunday Times Short Story Awards |date= 10 February 2017|language=en|url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170816023001/https://shortstoryaward.co.uk/articles/view/97|archive-date=16 August 2017}}</ref>

In 2013, [[Alice Munro]] was [[2013 Nobel Prize in Literature|awarded]] the [[Nobel Prize in Literature]] – her citation read: "master of the contemporary short story".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/2013/summary/|title=The Nobel Prize in Literature 2013|website=NobelPrize.org|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-16}}</ref> She said she hopes the award will bring readership for the short story, as well as recognising the short story for its own merit, rather than "something that people do before they write their first novel".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/2013/munro/25382-interview-with-alice-munro/|title=The Nobel Prize in Literature 2013|website=NobelPrize.org|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-16}}</ref> Short stories were cited in the choice of other laureates as well: [[Paul Heyse]] in 1910 and [[Gabriel García Márquez]] in 1982.<ref name="Literature1910">{{cite web|url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/literature/laureates/1910/index.html|title=Nobel Prize in Literature 1910|publisher=Nobel Foundation|access-date=2008-10-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081011192641/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/literature/laureates/1910/index.html|archive-date=2008-10-11|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Literature1982">{{cite web|url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/literature/laureates/1982/index.html|title=Nobel Prize in Literature 1982|publisher=Nobel Foundation|access-date=2008-10-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081017212833/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/literature/laureates/1982/index.html|archive-date=2008-10-17|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Adaptations==
Short stories are sometimes adapted for radio, TV or film:
* [[Radio drama]]s, as on ''[[NBC Presents: Short Story]]'' (1951–52). A popular example of this is "[[The Hitch-Hiker (radio play)|The Hitch-Hiker]]", read by [[Orson Welles]].
* [[Short film]]s, often rewritten by other writers, and even as feature films; such is the case of "[[Children of the Corn]]", "[[The Shawshank Redemption]]", "[[The Birds (story)|The Birds]]", "[[Brokeback Mountain]]", "[[Who Goes There?]]", "[[Duel (1971 film)|Duel]]", "[[A Sound of Thunder]]", "[[The Body (2001 film)|The Body]]", "[[Total Recall (1990 film)|Total Recall]]", "[[The Lawnmower Man]]", "[[Hearts in Atlantis]]", and "[[The Secret Life of Walter Mitty]]".
* [[Television special]]s, such as "[[12:01 P.M.]]" (a 1993 television movie), "[[Nightmare at 20,000 Feet]]" (an October 11, 1963, episode of ''[[The Twilight Zone]]''), "[[The Lottery]]", and "[[Button, Button (The Twilight Zone)|Button, Button]]" (on ''The Twilight Zone'').

==Characteristics==
As a concentrated, concise form of [[Narrative structure|narrative]] and descriptive prose fiction, the short story has been theorised about through the traditional elements of [[dramatic structure]]: '''exposition''' (the introduction of setting, situation, and main characters), '''complication''' (the event that introduces the conflict), [[Three-act structure#Structure|rising action]], '''crisis''' (the decisive moment for the protagonist and his commitment to a course of action), '''climax''' (the point of highest interest in terms of the conflict and the point with the most action) and '''resolution''' (the point when the conflict is resolved). Because of their length, short stories may or may not often follow this pattern. For example, modern short stories only occasionally have an exposition, more typically beginning in the middle of the action (''[[in medias res]]''). As with longer stories, plots of short stories also have a climax, crisis or turning point.{{Citation needed|date=August 2021}} In general, short stories feature endings which might be either conclusive or open-ended.{{Sfn|Young|2018|p=12}} Ambiguity is a recurrent trope in short stories; whether in their ending, characterisation or length.{{Sfn|Young|2018|p=13}} As with any art form, the exact characteristics of a short story will vary depending on who is its creator.{{Citation needed|date=August 2021}}

Characteristic of short story authors, according to professor of English, Clare Hanson, is that they are "losers and loners, exiles, women, blacks – writers who for one reason or another have not been part of the ruling 'narrative' or epistemological/experiential framework of their society".{{sfn|Young|2018|p=2}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Speculative fiction by writers of color
======================================================================

{{Short description|Speculative fiction created by nonwhite authors}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=March 2018}}

[[Speculative fiction]] is defined as [[science fiction]], [[fantasy]], and [[Horror fiction|horror]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About |url=https://speculativeliterature.org/about/ |website=Speculative Literature Foundation |language=en-US|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260103150321/https://speculativeliterature.org/about/|archive-date=January 3, 2026|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Brown|first=Kat|url=https://www.penguin.co.uk/discover/articles/what-is-speculative-fiction-genre-definition-books|title=A guide to speculative fiction|website=[[Penguin Books Limited]]|date=August 15, 2025|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260211071511/https://www.penguin.co.uk/discover/articles/what-is-speculative-fiction-genre-definition-books|archive-date=February 11, 2026|url-status=live}}</ref> Within those categories exists many other subcategories, for example [[cyberpunk]], [[magical realism]], and [[psychological horror]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |last=Carter |first=Heath W. |title=Speculative Fiction |date=March 29, 2017 |encyclopedia=Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Literature |url=https://oxfordre.com/literature/literature/display/10.1093/acrefore/9780190201098.001.0001/acrefore-9780190201098-e-78 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |doi=10.1093/acrefore/9780190201098.013.78 |isbn= |access-date=February 12, 2026 |via=[[Oxford Research Encyclopedias]] |quote=These include, but are not limited to, utopia, dystopia, eutopia, horror, the gothic, steampunk, slipstream, alternative history, cyberpunk, time slip, magic(al) realism, supernatural romance, weird fiction, the New Weird, (post)apocalyptic fiction, myth, legend, traditional, retold, and fractured fairy tale, folktale, ghost fiction, New Wave fabulation, and other interstitial genres|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

"[[Person of color]]" is a term used in the United States to denote non-[[white person]]s, sometimes narrowed to mean non-[[White Anglo-Saxon Protestant|WASP]] persons or [[non-Hispanic whites]], if "[[ethnic white]]s" are included.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Person of color {{!}} Research Starters {{!}} EBSCO Research |url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/person-color |website=[[EBSCO Information Services|EBSCO]] |language=en|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260103140435/https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/person-color|archive-date=January 3, 2026|url-status=live}}</ref> The term "person of color" is used to redefine what it means to be a part of the historically marginalized racial and ethnic groups within Western society. A writer of color is a writer who is a part of a marginalized culture in regards to traditional Euro-Western mainstream culture. This includes [[Asians]], African-Americans, Africans, [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]], Latinos, Asian Americans, and [[Pacific Islanders]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=People of color {{!}} Research Starters {{!}} EBSCO Research |url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/ethnic-and-cultural-studies/people-color |website=[[EBSCO Information Services|EBSCO]] |language=en|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260212202206/https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/ethnic-and-cultural-studies/people-color|archive-date=February 12, 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>

== African-American speculative fiction ==
{{Main|Black science fiction}}
Black science fiction or black speculative fiction is an umbrella term that covers a variety of activities within the [[science fiction]], [[fantasy]], and [[Horror fiction|horror]] genres where people of the African descent take part or are depicted. Some of its defining characteristics include a critique of the social structures leading to black oppression paired with an investment in social change.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tal|first=Kali|date=June 1, 2002|title="That Just Kills Me:" Black Militant Near-Future Fiction|journal=Social Text|language=en|volume=20|issue=2 71|pages=65–91|doi=10.1215/01642472-20-2_71-65|s2cid=145772884 |issn=0164-2472}}</ref> Black science fiction is "fed by technology but not led by it."<ref name=":2" /> This means that black science fiction often explores with human engagement with technology instead of technology as an innate good.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Onyebuchi|first=Tochi|url=https://www.tor.com/2018/02/27/homecoming-how-afrofuturism-bridges-the-past-and-the-present/|title=Homecoming: How Afrofuturism Bridges the Past and the Present|date=February 27, 2018|work=[[Tor.com]]|access-date=March 30, 2018|language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220623200032/https://www.tor.com/2018/02/27/homecoming-how-afrofuturism-bridges-the-past-and-the-present/|archive-date=June 23, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref> In the late 1990s a number of cultural critics began to use the term [[Afrofuturism]] to depict a cultural and literary movement of thinkers and artists of the African diaspora who were using science, technology, and science fiction as means of exploring the black experience.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Yazek|first=Lisa|date=November 2006|url=http://sdonline.org/42/afrofuturism-science-fiction-and-the-history-of-the-future/|title=Afrofuturism, Science Fiction, and the History of the Future|journal=[[Socialism and Democracy]]|volume=20|issue=1|issn=0885-4300}}</ref> However, as [[Nisi Shawl]] describes in her series on the history of black science fiction, black science fiction is a wide-ranging genre with a history reaching as far back as the 19th century.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Shawl |first=Nisi |url=https://carlbrandon.org/2020/01/crash-course-in-the-history-of-black-science-fiction-and-fantasy/ |title=A Crash Course in the History of Black Science Fiction|work=[[Carl Brandon Society]]|date=January 30, 2020|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250315173428/https://carlbrandon.org/2020/01/crash-course-in-the-history-of-black-science-fiction-and-fantasy/|archive-date=March 15, 2025|url-status=live}}</ref> Also, because of the interconnections between black culture and black science fiction, "readers and critics need first to be familiar with the traditions of African American literature and culture" in order to correctly interpret the nuances of the texts.<ref name=":2" /> Indeed, John Pfeiffer has argued that there have always been elements of speculative fiction in black literature.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Pfeiffer|first=John|date=December 1, 1975|title=Black American Speculative Literature|journal=Extrapolation|volume=17|issue=1|pages=35–43|doi=10.3828/extr.1975.17.1.35|issn=0014-5483}}</ref> Hope Wabuke, a writer and assistant professor at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] of English and Creative Writing, argues that the term "Black Speculative Literature" can encompass the terms Afrofuturism, [[Africanfuturism]], and Africanjujuism, the latter two coined by [[Nnedi Okorafor]], all of which center "African and African diasporic culture, thought, mythos, philosophy, and worldviews."<ref name="wabuke">{{Cite web|last=Wabuke|first=Hope|title=Afrofuturism, Africanfuturism, and the Language of Black Speculative Literature|url=https://lareviewofbooks.org/article/afrofuturism-africanfuturism-and-the-language-of-black-speculative-literature/|date=August 27, 2020|work=[[LA Review of Books]]|access-date=February 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200829112202/https://lareviewofbooks.org/article/afrofuturism-africanfuturism-and-the-language-of-black-speculative-literature/|archive-date=29 August 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Arab speculative fiction ==
{{Main|Arab speculative fiction}}

Arab speculative fiction is speculative fiction written by Arabic authors that commonly portrays themes of repression, cyclical violence, and the concept of a utopia long lost by years of destruction.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Alter |first=Alexandra |date=2016-05-29 |title=Middle Eastern Writers Find Refuge in the Dystopian Novel |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/30/books/middle-eastern-writers-find-refuge-in-the-dystopian-novel.html |access-date=April 8, 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Arabic-American speculative fiction is portrayed through the involvement of the United States in the country-specific subgenres of Arabic speculative fiction. Culture specific subgenres have their own distinct themes from one another characterized by the experiences of those within their respective states. Two such states, the land referred to as [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]], and [[Egypt]], each have themes specific to their individual histories and cultural experiences.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last=El Shakry |first=Hoda |date=July 4, 2021 |title=Palestine and the Aesthetics of the Future Impossible |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1369801X.2021.1885471 |journal=Interventions |language=en |volume=23 |issue=5 |pages=669–690 |doi=10.1080/1369801X.2021.1885471 |issn=1369-801X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Marusek |first=Sarah |date=October 20, 2022 |title=Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow: social justice and the rise of dystopian art and literature post-Arab Uprisings |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13530194.2020.1853504 |journal=British Journal of Middle Eastern Studies |language=en |volume=49 |issue=5 |pages=747–768 |doi=10.1080/13530194.2020.1853504 |issn=1353-0194|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Examples of themes in Palestinian speculative fiction include settler occupation, lost futures, and stoicism in the face of opposition, while themes in Egyptian speculative fiction include militant governments, repressed uprisings, and totalitarianism.<ref name=":1"/><ref name=":02" />

== Asian and Asian American speculative fiction ==
While the term [[Afrofuturism]] is widely used and accepted to explain the mingling of the African American experience with technology, science, and the future, a similar term, "Asianfuturism," has yet to catch on.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 27, 2020 |title=Musings on Asianfuturism? – ED(MOND)CHANG(ED)AGOGY |url=http://www.edmondchang.com/2020/04/27/musings-on-asianfuturism/ |access-date=April 27, 2024 |language=en-US}}</ref> Popularity is growing for English translations of [[Chinese science fiction]] novels, but the number of Asian-American science fiction authors remains small and underrepresented.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A Reflection on Chinese and Asian American Representation in Sci-Fi and Fantasy |url=https://www.sfwp.com/quarterly/a-reflection-on-chinese-and-asian-american-representation-in-sci-fi-and-fantasy |access-date=April 27, 2024 |website=Santa Fe Writers Project |language=en-US}}</ref> Women's experiences are also explored through the lens of [[cyberpunk]] fiction, with an emphasis on the female body.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |title=Techno-Orientalism: imagining Asia in speculative fiction, history, and media |date=2015 |publisher=Rutgers University Press |isbn=978-0-8135-7064-8 |editor-last=Roh |editor-first=David S. |series=Asian American studies today |location=New Brunswick, New Jersey |editor-last2=Huang |editor-first2=Betsy |editor-last3=Niu |editor-first3=Greta A.}}</ref>

=== Japanese speculative fiction ===
{{Main|Japanese science fiction}}
[[Science fiction]]  is an important genre of modern [[Japanese literature]] that has strongly influenced aspects of contemporary Japanese pop culture, including [[anime]], [[manga]], [[video games]], [[tokusatsu]], and [[Cinema of Japan|cinema]]. Japanese fiction has assumed a position of significance in many genres of world literature, with speculative fiction encompassing a diverse range of literary works, has a rich history deeply intertwined with the country's cultural and social contexts, It is Often characterized by its imaginative narratives, futuristic themes, and exploration of societal issues,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schnellbächer |first=Thomas |date=2002 |title=Has the Empire Sunk Yet? The Pacific in Japanese Science Fiction |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4241106 |journal=Science Fiction Studies |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=382–396 |doi=10.1525/sfs.29.3.0382 |jstor=4241106 |issn=0091-7729}}</ref> It has gained international recognition for its unique blend of traditional storytelling elements with modern speculative concepts. Contemporary Japanese speculative fiction has themes focusing on artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, and environmental degradation are prevalent, reflecting the anxieties and realities of the modern world.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cordasco |first=Rachel |title=Out of This World: Speculative Fiction in Translation from the Cold War to the New Millennium |date=2021 |publisher=University of Illinois Press |isbn=9780252052910}}</ref>

==== Japanese horror ====
{{Main|Japanese horror}}
Belief in [[ghosts]], [[demons]] and spirits has been deep-rooted in [[Japanese folklore]] throughout history. It is entwined with mythology and superstition derived from Japanese [[Shinto]], as well as [[Buddhism]] and [[Taoism]] brought to Japan from China and [[India]]. Stories and legends, combined with mythology, have been collected over the years by various cultures of the world, both past and present. Folklore has evolved in order to explain or rationalize various natural events. Inexplicable phenomena arouse a fear in humankind because there is no way for us to anticipate them or to understand their origins.<ref name="rubin">{{cite web |last=Rubin |first=Norman A. |date=June 26, 2000 |title=Ghosts, Demons and Spirits in Japanese Lore |url=https://asianart.com/articles/rubin/ |website=Asianart.com}}</ref> The early horror stories of Japan (also known as [[Kaidan (parapsychology)|Kaidan]] or more recently [[J-Horror]]) revolved around vengeful spirits or [[Yūrei]]. In recent years, interest in these tales have been revived with the release of such films as ''[[Ju-on: The Grudge]]'' and ''[[Ring (film)|Ring]]'' .<ref>Orenstein, C. & Cusack, T. (2024). ''Puppet and spirit: Ritual, religion, and performing objects: Volume II''. London: Routledge. DOI: 10.4324/9781003150589</ref>{{citation needed|date=December 2024}}

=== Chinese American speculative fiction ===
{{Main|Chinese American speculative fiction}}
Chinese American speculative fiction is speculative fiction written by [[Chinese-American]] authors that many speculative works by [[Asian American]] authors delve into the immigrant experience, addressing themes of displacement, assimilation, and the search for belonging in a new land. Like speculative fiction in general, Chinese American speculative fiction often serves as a platform for social commentary. It may address current issues such as racism, discrimination, environmental degradation, and political unrest through the lens of speculative elements.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Esaki |first=Brett J. |date=22 January 2020 |title=Ted Chiang's Asian American Amusement at Alien Arrival |journal=Religions |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=56 |doi=10.3390/rel11020056 |doi-access=free |hdl=10150/641210 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Chinese American speculative fiction written by and about women work on creating the feeling of nostalgia in readers, focusing in on experiences by second-generation Americans.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gullander-Drolet |first=Claire |date=2021 |title=Imperialist Nostalgia and Untranslatable Affect in Ling Ma's Severance |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/pub/347/article/800359 |journal=Science Fiction Studies |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=94–108 |doi=10.1353/sfs.2021.0024 |issn=2327-6207|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Indian speculative fiction ===
{{see also||Bengali science fiction|
Category:Indian speculative fiction|
Kalpabiswa|So Long Been Dreaming}}
[[File:Anil Menon (author).jpg|thumb|[[Anil Menon (writer)|Anil Menon]], Indian science fiction author known for his novels "The Beast With Nine Billion Feet" and "Half of What I Say" as well as his contributions to many short story anthologies]]
Indian speculative fiction has had long-standing roots with the earliest known examples being published in 1835. Early authors such as [[Henry Meredith Parker]], [[Henry Goodeve]], Kylas Chunder Dutt, Soshee Chunder Dutt, [[Begum Rokeya|Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain]], and [[Jagadish Chandra Bose]] helped develop the genre.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Science Fiction in Colonial India, 1835–1905 |url=https://anthempress.com/humanities-literature-and-arts/science-fiction-in-colonial-india-1835-1905-pdf |access-date=April 26, 2024 |website=AnthemPress |language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240424160023/https://anthempress.com/humanities-literature-and-arts/science-fiction-in-colonial-india-1835-1905-pdf|archive-date=April 24, 2024|url-status=live}}</ref> From "The Junction of the Ocean: A Tale of the Year 2098", a story of how the construction of the Panama Canal changed the landscape of the world<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parker |first=Henry Meredith |date=1835 |title="The Junction of the Ocean. A Tale of the Year 2098" |url=https://openpublishing.psu.edu/utopia/content/%E2%80%9C-junction-ocean-tale-year-2098%E2%80%9D |access-date=April 26, 2025 |website=openpublishing.psu.edu|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241103000836/https://openpublishing.psu.edu/utopia/content/%E2%80%9C-junction-ocean-tale-year-2098%E2%80%9D|archive-date=November 3, 2024}}</ref> to "The Republic of Orissá; A Page from the Annals of the Twentieth Century”, a dystopia about a revolt against Britain's institutionalization of a law supporting slavery on colonial India, and "Sultana's Dream", a feminist utopia in where traditional gender norms are turned on their head,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sultana's Dream. |url=https://digital.library.upenn.edu/women/sultana/dream/dream.html |access-date=April 26, 2024 |website=digital.library.upenn.edu|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260212005439/https://digital.library.upenn.edu/women/sultana/dream/dream.html|archive-date=February 12, 2026|url-status=live}}</ref> as well as, "Runaway Cyclone", about a man who calmed a sea storm using hair oil, which anticipated the phenomenon known as the "[[butterfly effect]],"<ref>{{Cite web |last=words |first=Anil MenonBy: Vandana Singh Issue: 30 September 2013 1139 |date=September 30, 2013 |title=Introduction to "Runaway Cyclone" and "Sheesha Ghat" these authors' contributions bring unique perspectives on imperial and anti-imperial sentiments during colonial times.<ref name=":2" /> With recent twisted in the genre, stories present a different take for readers to appreciate.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2021-03-23 |title=Perspective {{!}} Let's talk about wonderful Indian science-fiction and fantasy novels |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/entertainment/books/lets-talk-about-wonderful-indian-science-fiction-and-fantasy-novels/2021/03/22/ff61b888-868a-11eb-8a8b-5cf82c3dffe4_story.html |access-date=April 24, 2024 |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286 |archive-date=May 20, 2022}}</ref>

== Latino/Latinx speculative fiction  ==
{{see also|Latinofuturism|Chicanafuturism}}
{{expand section|date=February 2026}}
Speculative fiction by authors in the Latino community explores environmental and social issues, ethnicity, diaspora, ethnicity, and other issues.<ref>{{cite web|last=Oliva|first=Alejandra|url=https://remezcla.com/lists/culture/sci-fi-books-latino-authors/|title=5 Books by Latino Authors That Will Satisfy Sci-Fi Junkies|website=[[Remezcla]]|date=June 12, 2018|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240418202928/https://remezcla.com/lists/culture/sci-fi-books-latino-authors/|archive-date=April 18, 2024|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Rowland|first=Rey|url=https://bookriot.com/latine-science-fiction-and-fantasy/|title=12 Latine SFF Books You Definitely Should Read|website=Book Riot|date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250722070342/https://bookriot.com/latine-science-fiction-and-fantasy/ |archive-date=July 22, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Gil’Adí |first=Maia |editor-last1=Orchard |editor-first1=William |date=June 19, 2025 |title=Latinx Literature in Transition, 1992–2020 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/latinx-literature-in-transition-1992-2020/B67AD63F47679D1686BFDAE5A87BE9B5 |chapter=Chapter 10 - Latinx Speculative Fiction, Speculative Latinx |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/latinx-literature-in-transition-19922020/latinx-speculative-fiction-speculative-latinx/B943A23EA0AFA5C02D0AB5D2535F6E3F |location=Cambridge |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |page= |isbn=9781009314091 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250621024147/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/latinx-literature-in-transition-19922020/latinx-speculative-fiction-speculative-latinx/B943A23EA0AFA5C02D0AB5D2535F6E3F |archive-date=June 21, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026}}</ref> At the same time, countries like [[Mexico]] have their own traditions of speculative narratives, with Latin America having a "rich diversity" of speculative stories.<ref>{{cite web|last=Chimal|first=Alberto|url=https://latinamericanliteraturetoday.org/2018/05/latin-american-speculative-fiction-alberto-chimal/|title=On Latin American Speculative Fiction|website=Latin American Literature Today|date=May 2018|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251205122450/https://latinamericanliteraturetoday.org/2018/05/latin-american-speculative-fiction-alberto-chimal/|archive-date=December 5, 2025|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Hernandez|first=Carlos|url=https://mithilareview.com/latin_american_sf_01_2017/|title=Latin American Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror: A Round Table Discussion|website=Mithila Review|date=January 5, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251107154406/https://mithilareview.com/latin_american_sf_01_2017/ |archive-date=November 7, 2025 |access-date=February 12, 2026}}</ref>

Latino literature scholar Renee Hudson stated that "speculative imaginaries" are limited by contradictions inherent in [[Latinidad]], which some scholars described as incoherent, and noted that Latinx speculative fictions are "not immune from colonizer imaginaries," while stating that such fictions can "move beyond nationalistic frameworks" and called them a toolkit for a "more just, anti-racist world and a more expansive, inclusive latinidad."<ref>{{cite web|last=Hudson|first=Renee|url=https://asapjournal.com/feature/imagining-the-futures-of-latinx-speculative-fictions-renee-hudson/|title=Imagining the Futures of Latinx Speculative Fictions|website=ASAP Review|date=December 2, 2019|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251109214441/https://asapjournal.com/feature/imagining-the-futures-of-latinx-speculative-fictions-renee-hudson/|archive-date=November 9, 2025|url-status=live}}</ref>

Several books have been published on this subject, including ''Altermundos: Latin@ Speculative Literature, Film, and Popular Culture'', ''Latinx Rising: An Anthology of Latinx Science Fiction and Fantasy'' and ''Speculative Fiction for Dreamers: A Latinx Anthology'', noting the focus of this fiction on [[modernity]], [[immigration]], [[globalization]], identity, [[colonialism]], [[gender]], and [[Race (human categorization)|race]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.chicano.ucla.edu/publications/book/altermundos|title=Altermundos: Latin@ Speculative Literature, Film, and Popular Culture|website=UCLA Chicano Studies Research Center|publisher=[[UCLA]]|date=April 2017|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251110224130/https://www.chicano.ucla.edu/publications/book/altermundos|archive-date=November 10, 2025|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ohiostatepress.org/books/titles/9780814257982.html|title=Speculative Fiction for Dreamers: A Latinx Anthology|website=Ohio State University Press|publisher=[[Ohio State University]]|date=September 2021|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251118000816/https://ohiostatepress.org/books/titles/9780814257982.html|archive-date=November 18, 2025|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://ohiostatepress.org/books/titles/9780814255896.html|title=Latinx Rising: An Anthology of Latinx Science Fiction and Fantasy|website=Ohio State University Press|publisher=[[Ohio State University]]|date=September 2021|access-date=February 12, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251008062016/https://ohiostatepress.org/books/titles/9780814255896.html|archive-date=October 8, 2025|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Indigenous speculative fiction of North America==
{{see|Indigenous futurisms|Two-spirit#Speculative fiction and media|Native American literature}}
Many [[Indigenous writers of the Americas]] write speculative fiction, including [[Native Americans in the United States]] [[Indigenous peoples in Canada]], and [[Greenlandic Inuit]]. There is also categorical overlap between many [[Latine people]] and [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas]].

[[Indigenous futurisms]] is a widespread movement, related to [[Afrofuturism]] and science fiction, that involves Indigenous peoples imagining possible futures through fiction.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Adams |first1=James Ring |title=Arts and Cultures Native Authors Invade Sci-Fi: Indigenous Writers are Reshaping Speculative Fiction |url=https://www.americanindianmagazine.org/story/native-authors-invade-scifi |access-date=12 February 2026 |work=American Indian |agency=Smithsonian Institution |volume=20 |issue=4 |publisher=National Museum of the American Indian |date=Winter 2019}}</ref>

[[Two-Spirit]] speculative fiction is a genre that explores [[gender identity]] and cultural perspectives through Indigenous traditions and futuristic or [[Alternate history|alternate realities]], sometimes empowering and inspiring readers. The genre offers Indigenous authors and readers a chance to express, reclaim, and reshape their narratives while questioning conventional views on gender and culture through fictional stories.<ref>{{Citation |last=Pearson |first=Wendy Gay |title=Speculative Fiction and Queer Theory |date=October 19, 2022 |encyclopedia=Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Communication |url=https://oxfordre.com/communication/display/10.1093/acrefore/9780190228613.001.0001/acrefore-9780190228613-e-1214 |access-date=May 1, 2024 |language=en |doi=10.1093/acrefore/9780190228613.013.1214 |isbn=978-0-19-022861-3|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The emergence of Two-Spirit speculative fiction can be understood in the context of [[LGBT literature|queer literature]]'s broader landscape. This includes its efforts to challenge [[Heteronormativity|heteronormative]] narratives and enhance representation within the [[LGBT community|LGBTQ+ community]]. Two-Spirit authors use their writing to assert their independence from settler counter-parts and envision a better future for themselves and their communities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Two-Spirit |url=https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/two-spirit |access-date=April 23, 2015 |website=[[The Canadian Encyclopedia]] |language=en |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220331215324/https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/two-spirit/|archive-date=March 31, 2022|url-status=live}}</ref>

Such works are also characterized by a sense of optimism and hope for the future, contrasting with the dark history of Indigenous peoples in the Americas, marked by destruction and [[genocide]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Elm |first1=Jessica H. L. |last2=Lewis |first2=Jordan P. |last3=Walters |first3=Karina L. |last4=Self |first4=Jen M. |date=2016 |title="I'm in this World for a Reason": Resilience and recovery among American Indian and Alaska Native Two Spirit Women |journal=Journal of Lesbian Studies |volume=20 |issue=3–4 |pages=352–371 |doi=10.1080/10894160.2016.1152813 |issn=1089-4160 |pmc=6424359 |pmid=27254761}}</ref>

'''Thomas Michael Disch''' (February 2, 1940 – July 4, 2008) was an American [[science fiction writer]] and poet.<ref name="schudel2008">{{cite news |first=Matt |last=Schudel |title=Thomas Disch; sci-fi writer was part of 'New Wave' |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/story/2008/07/09/ST2008070901926.html |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |page=B05 |date=July 9, 2008 |access-date=2008-07-12}}</ref><ref name="Martin0708">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/07/08/books/08disch.html |title=Thomas Disch, Novelist, Dies at 68 |first=Douglas |last=Martin |date=July 8, 2008 |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=2008-08-04}}</ref><ref name="stewart2008">{{cite news |first=Jocelyn Y. |last=Stewart |title=Thomas M. Disch, 68; prolific science-fiction author |url=http://www.latimes.com/news/printedition/california/la-me-disch8-2008jul08,0,2416990.story |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=July 8, 2008 |access-date=2008-07-12 |quote=fatally shot himself in the head July 5, according to the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.}}</ref> He won the [[Hugo Award]] for Best Related Book—previously called "Best Non-Fiction Book"—in 1999. He had two other Hugo nominations and nine [[Nebula Award]] nominations to his credit, plus one win of the [[John W. Campbell Memorial Award]], a [[Rhysling Award]], and two [[Seiun Award]]s, among others.

In the 1960s, his work began appearing in science-fiction magazines. His critically acclaimed science fiction novels, ''[[The Genocides]]'', ''[[Camp Concentration]]'' and ''[[334 (novel)|334]]'' are major contributions to the [[New Wave (science fiction)|New Wave]] science fiction movement. In 1996, his book ''The Castle of Indolence: On Poetry, Poets, and Poetasters'' was nominated for the [[National Book Critics Circle Award]],<ref name=bionote /> and in 1999, Disch won the Nonfiction Hugo for ''[[The Dreams Our Stuff Is Made Of]]'', a meditation on the impact of science fiction on culture, as well as the [[Michael Braude Award for Light Verse]]. Among his other nonfiction work, he wrote theatre and opera criticism for ''[[The New York Times]]'', ''[[The Nation (U.S. periodical)|The Nation]]'', and other periodicals. He published several volumes of poetry as Tom Disch.

Following an extended period of depression after the death in 2005 of his life-partner, Charles Naylor, Disch stopped writing almost entirely, except for poetry and blog entries, although he did produce two novellas.<ref name=bionote /> Disch fatally [[Suicide methods#Shooting|shot himself]] on July 4, 2008, in his apartment in [[Manhattan]], New York City.<ref name=bionote /><ref name="schudel2008" /><ref name="Martin0708" /> Naylor and Disch are buried alongside each other at Saint Johns Episcopal Church Columbarium, [[Dubuque, Iowa]]. His last book, ''The Word of God'', which was written shortly before Naylor died, had just been published a few days before Disch's death.<ref name=bionote /> His last short story collection, ''The Wall of America'', Disch's first in over 25 years, was published posthumously several months later.  In  a special 2024 edition,  ''New Worlds'', which had published much of his best science fiction, published the first few chapters of his unfinished science fiction comedy ''Peanut and Buster'' on the theme of humans and elephants marrying, riffing off the statement of a baseball-playing super-Christian's remarks about gay marriage.

== Early life ==
Disch was born in [[Des Moines, Iowa|Des Moines]], Iowa, on February 2, 1940. Because of a [[polio]] epidemic in 1946, his mother Helen [[homeschooling|home-schooled]] him for a year. As a result, he skipped from [[kindergarten]] to second grade. Disch's first formal education was at Catholic schools, as evidenced in some of his works which contain scathing criticisms of the Catholic Church. The family moved in 1953 to St. Paul in [[Minnesota]], rejoining both pairs of grandparents, where Disch attended both public and [[Parochial schools|Catholic]] schools.<ref name="bionote">"Biographical note" in Disch, Thomas M. ''The Wall of America''. San Francisco: [[Tachyon Publications|Tachyon]], 2008. {{ISBN|1-892391-82-1}}, pp. 244–245.</ref> In the Saint Paul public schools, Disch discovered his long-term loves of science fiction, drama, and poetry. He describes poetry as his stepping-stone to the literary world. A teacher at St. Paul Central, Jeannette Cochran, assigned 100 lines of poetry to be memorized; Disch wound up memorizing ten times as much.<ref name="heacox">{{citation |last=Heacox |first=Tom |title=The Dish on Tom Disch |periodical=Jump! Magazine |date=Fall 1995 |publisher=[[The College of William and Mary]] |access-date=2004-02-29 |url=http://web.wm.edu/so/jump/fall95/disch.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080914125423/http://web.wm.edu/so/jump/fall95/disch.html |archive-date=September 14, 2008 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> His early fascination continued to influence his work with poetic form and the direction of his criticism.

After graduating from high school in 1957, he worked a summer job as a trainee steel [[technical drawing|draftsman]], just one of the many jobs on his path to becoming a writer. Saving enough to move to New York City at the age of 17,<ref name=bionote /> he found a [[Manhattan]] apartment and began to cast his energies in many directions. He worked as an extra at the [[Metropolitan Opera|Metropolitan Opera House]] in productions of ''[[Spartacus (ballet)|Spartacus]]'' for the [[Bolshoi Ballet]], ''[[Swan Lake]]'' for the [[Royal Ballet]], and ''[[Don Giovanni]]'', ''[[Tosca]]'' and others for the [[Metropolitan Opera|Met]].<ref name=word>Disch, Thomas M. ''The Word of God''. San Francisco: Tachyon, 2008, p.68-69.</ref> He found work at a bookstore, then at a newspaper. At the age of 18, a penniless, friendless teenager, he attempted suicide by gas oven but survived due to not having had enough money to pay the gas bill.<ref>Disch, Thomas M. ''The Word of God''. San Francisco: Tachyon, 2008. p.26.</ref>  Later that year, he enlisted in the army. Disch's incompatibility with the armed forces quickly resulted in a nearly three-month commitment to a [[mental hospital]].

After his discharge, Disch returned to New York and continued to pursue the arts in his own indirect way. He worked, again, in bookstores, and as a copywriter.<ref name=bionote /> Some of these jobs later paid off; working as a cloak room attendant in New York theater culture allowed him to both pursue his lifelong love of drama and led to work as a reviewer of staged drama. Eventually, he got another job with an insurance company and went to school. A brief flirtation with architecture led him to apply to [[Cooper Union]], where he was told he got the highest score ever on their entrance exam, but he dropped out after a few weeks.<ref name=word /> He then went to night school at [[New York University]] (NYU), where classes on novella writing and [[utopian]] fiction developed his tastes for some of the common forms and topics of science fiction. In May 1962, he decided to write a short story instead of studying for his midterm exams.<ref name=bionote /> He sold the story, "The Double Timer", for $112.50 to the magazine ''[[Fantastic (magazine)|Fantastic]]''.<ref name=bionote /><ref name="francaville">{{citation |last=Francavilla |first=Joeseph |title=Disching It Out: An Interview with Thomas Disch |periodical=Science Fiction Studies |volume=37 |year=1985 |pages=241–251}}</ref> Having begun his literary career, he did not return to NYU but rather took another series of odd jobs such as [[bank teller]], [[mortuary]] assistant, and copy editor—all of which served to fuel what he referred to as his night-time "writing habit". Over the next few years he wrote more science fiction stories but also branched out into poetry; his first published poem, "Echo and Narcissus", appeared in the ''[[Minnesota Review]]'''s Summer 1964 issue.<ref name="davis">{{citation |last=Davis |first=Matthew S. S. |title=Schrödinger's Cake |date=December 28, 2001 |access-date=2004-03-09 |url=http://www.ukjarry1.talktalk.net/tmd.htm |archive-date=February 6, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100206022502/http://www.ukjarry1.talktalk.net/tmd.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Career ==
Disch entered the field of science fiction at a turning point, as the [[pulp adventure]] stories of its older style began to be challenged by a more serious, darker style. Rather than trying to compete with mainstream writers on the New York literary scene, Disch published work in science fiction and literary magazines, and began to speak with a new voice. His first novel, ''[[The Genocides]]'', appeared in 1965; [[Brian W. Aldiss]] singled it out for praise in a long review in [[Science Fantasy (magazine)|''SF Impulse'']].<ref>"Book Fare," [[Science Fantasy (magazine)|''SF Impulse'']], January 1967, p.51-54.</ref> Much of his early science fiction was published in English author [[Michael Moorcock]]'s New Wave magazine, ''[[New Worlds (magazine)|New Worlds]]'', including his sixth novel ''[[Camp Concentration]]'' in three installments.  His reputation in the U.K. was very high and he was ranked with Ballard, Moorcock and Aldiss as a leading writer of literary fantastika.

Disch traveled widely and lived in England, Spain, Rome, and Mexico. In spite of this, he remained a New Yorker for the last twenty years of his life, keeping a long-time New York residence overlooking Union Square. He said that "a city like New York, to my mind, is the whole world."<ref name="horwich" />

Writing had become the dominant focus of his life. Disch described his personal transformation from dilettante to "someone who knows what he wants to do and is so busy doing it that he doesn't have much time for anything else."<ref name="heacox" /> After ''The Genocides'', he wrote ''[[Camp Concentration]]'' and ''[[334 (novel)|334]]''. More books followed, including science fiction novels and stories, [[Gothic novel|gothic]] works, criticism, plays, a [[libretto]] for an opera of ''[[Frankenstein]]'', prose and verse children's books such as ''A Child's Garden of Grammar'', and ten poetry collections. In the 1980s, he moved from science fiction to horror with a quartet set in Minneapolis: ''[[The Businessman: A Tale of Terror|The Businessman]]'', ''The M.D.'', ''The Priest'', and ''The Sub''.

His writing includes substantial periodical work, such as regular book and theater reviews for ''[[The Nation (U.S. periodical)|The Nation]]'', ''[[The Weekly Standard]]'', ''[[Harper's]]'', ''[[The Washington Post]]'', the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', ''The New York Times'', the ''Times Literary Supplement'', and ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''. Recognition from his award-winning books led to a year as "artist-in-residence" at the [[College of William & Mary]]. During his long and varied career, Disch found his way into other forms and genres. As a fiction writer and a poet, Disch felt typecast by his science fiction roots. "I have a class theory of literature. I come from the wrong neighborhood to sell to ''The New Yorker''. No matter how good I am as an artist, they always can smell where I come from."<ref name="horwich">{{citation |title=Interview: Thomas M. Disch |first=David |last=Horwich |url=http://www.strangehorizons.com/2001/20010730/interview.shtml |periodical=[[Strange Horizons]] |date=July 30, 2001 |access-date=2007-11-04 |archive-date=November 3, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071103191237/http://www.strangehorizons.com/2001/20010730/interview.shtml |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Though Disch was an admirer of and friends with the author [[Philip K. Dick]],<ref>Although in his poem "Ode on the Death of Philip K. Dick", published in ''Here I Am, There You Are, Where Were We'' (Hutchinson, 1984), Disch writes of Dick: "I scarcely knew the man". In the semi-fictional semi-autobiographical ''The Word of God'' (2008), he writes that he only met Dick one time, when he visited him in Dick's condo in [[Anaheim, California|Anaheim]].</ref> Dick wrote an infamous paranoid letter to the [[FBI]] in October 1972 that denounced Disch and suggested that there were coded messages, prompted by a covert organization, in Disch's novel ''Camp Concentration''. Disch was unaware of this letter at the time, and he would go on to champion the [[Philip K. Dick Award]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.strangehorizons.com/2008/20080922/miller-a.shtml|title=Who Killed Thomas M. Disch?|first=Sam J.|last=Miller|date=September 22, 2008|work=Strange Horizons|access-date=March 13, 2010|archive-date=January 3, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100103095306/http://strangehorizons.com/2008/20080922/miller-a.shtml|url-status=dead}}</ref> However, in his final novel, ''The Word of God'', Disch got his revenge with a story in which Dick is in [[Hell]], unable to write because of [[writer's block]]. In return for a taste of human blood, which will unlock his ability to write, he makes a deal to go back in time and kill Disch's father so that Disch will never be born, and at the same time to kill [[Thomas Mann]] and thereby to ensure that [[Hitler]] wins [[World War II|World War&nbsp;II]]. Disch also referred to Dick in a blog post stating "May he rot in hell, and may his royalties corrupt his heirs to the seventh generation."<ref name="strangehorizons.com">{{Cite web|url=http://strangehorizons.com/non-fiction/articles/who-killed-thomas-m-disch/|title = Who Killed Thomas M. Disch?|date = September 22, 2008}}</ref>

Disch shared his Manhattan apartment and a house in [[Barryville, New York]], with his partner of three decades, poet and fiction writer Charles Naylor. Although he was [[Coming out|out]] as a gay man after 1968 and this facet of his life was occasionally foregrounded in his work (most notably in his poetry and ''On Wings of Song''), he did not try to write to a particular community: "I'm gay myself, but I don't write 'gay' literature."<ref name="horwich"/> He rarely mentioned his sexuality in interviews, though he was interviewed by the Canadian gay periodical ''[[The Body Politic (magazine)|The Body Politic]]'' in 1981.<ref>{{Citation | last1 = Galbraith | first1 = David | last2 = Wilson | first2 = Alexander | title = Taking flight with Thomas Disch | journal = The Body Politic | issue = December 1981 | pages = 26–28 }}</ref> After Naylor's death in 2005, Disch had to abandon the house, as well as fight attempts to evict him from his [[rent control]]led apartment<!--- reference Ellen Datlow's blog reporting circumstances of his death, http://ellen-datlow.livejournal.com/93886.html but hope for better citeable sources shortly --->, and he became steadily more depressed. He wrote on a [[LiveJournal]] account from April 2006 until his death, in which he posted poetry and journal entries.<ref>[http://tomsdisch.livejournal.com Disch's blog] at [[LiveJournal]]</ref> In September and October 2007, shortly before Disch's death, literary critic [[Peter Swirski]] conducted email interviews with Disch concerning his novels ''The M.D. A Horror Story'' and ''334''. Excerpts from these exchanges were published in Swirski's 2010 study ''Literature, Analytically Speaking''&nbsp;&ndash; Chapter 7 is mostly on ''The M.D.''&nbsp;&ndash; with Disch responding to questions with wit and irony.<ref>[[Peter Swirski|Swirski, Peter]] (2010) ''Literature, Analytically Speaking: Explorations in the Theory of Interpretation, Analytic Aesthetics, and Evolution'' University of Texas Press  {{ISBN|0292721781}}</ref>

Disch was an outspoken atheist<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nysun.com/obituaries/thomas-m-disch-68-eclectic-writer-of-science/81378/|title=Thomas M. Disch, 68, Eclectic Writer of Science Fiction|first=Stephen|last=Miller|date=July 8, 2008|work=[[The New York Sun]]}}</ref> as well as a satirist;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/bookreviews/3563693/The-Wall-of-America-by-Thomas-M-Disch.html|title=The Wall of America by Thomas M Disch|author-link=Michael Moorcock|first=Michael|last=Moorcock|date=November 26, 2008|work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]}}</ref> his last novel ''The Word of God'' was published by [[Tachyon Publications]] in the summer of 2008.<ref name="strangehorizons.com"/> His final published work, the posthumous story collection ''The Wall of America'', contains speculative fiction from the last half of Disch's career. Most of his literary short fiction was not collected after 1976 (although a story from ''The Hudson Review'' was collected in 2008). Right up to the end of his life, he maintained an active blog notable for its wit.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://blog.bestamericanpoetry.com/the_best_american_poetry/2020/12/tom-disch-what.html|title = Tom Disch: "God's Big Giveaway!"}}</ref>

===Computer game design===
{{Main|Amnesia (1986 video game)}}
[[File:Thomas Disch with computer and Amnesia game.jpg|right|thumb|Disch with his computer and ''Amnesia'' in 1986 or 1988]]
In 1986, Disch collaborated with [[New Jersey]] software company [[Cognetics Corporation]] and games publisher [[Electronic Arts]] to create the [[interactive fiction]] game ''[[Amnesia (1986 video game)|Amnesia]]'' for the [[Commodore 64]], [[IBM PC compatible]]s, and [[Apple II|Apple&nbsp;II]] computers. The game, based on technology pioneered by Cognetics' Charles Kreitzberg, was produced by [[Don Daglow]] and programmed by Kevin Bentley. It showcased Disch's vivid writing, a stark contrast to other game-programmer-written text adventures of the time, and his passion for the energy of the city of New York. Although the text adventure format was dying by the time ''Amnesia'' was released and it enjoyed limited success, the game pioneered ideas that would later become popular in game design by modeling the entire Manhattan street map south of 110th St. and allowing the player to visit any street corner in that part of the city in their quest to advance the story. Although the limited [[floppy disk]] capacity of the 1980s computers caused much of Disch's original text about the city to be cut, many Manhattan sites and people were described with unique loving distortion through the Disch lens. David Lehman singled out "Amnesia" for praise in his essay "You Are What You Read" in ''Newsweek'' (January 12, 1987). In an interview Lehman asked Disch about the origin of "Amnesia." "Please don't say 'I forget'," Lehman said. "It's true," Disch replied. "I forget my own life all the time, so amnesia was a natural subject for me."<ref>Southwest Review, vol. 73, no. 2 (Spring 1988)</ref>

===Theater===
Disch was also known for his work in the theater, both as the critic for ''The Nation'', from 1987 to 1993,<ref name=bionote /> and as writer of two performance works, his meta-historical stage adaptation of ''Ben-Hur'' and his controversial verse monologue/poem, ''The Cardinal Detoxes''. Both plays were commissioned and presented by Jeff Cohen and the RAPP Arts Center in New York's [[Alphabet City, Manhattan|Alphabet City]]. ''Ben-Hur'' not only told the story of the famous Biblical novel but delved into the life and times of its author, General [[Lew Wallace]]. Disch proffers the theory that Wallace penned ''Ben-Hur'', in part, to assuage his guilt over his role in the execution of [[Mary Surratt]]. In its world-premiere performance at the [[Peabody Conservatory]] in [[Baltimore]] in 1989, it was chosen as a Critics' Choice by ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine.

''The Cardinal Detoxes'' had a simple conceit: a Catholic bishop has committed vehicular homicide while driving intoxicated and is imprisoned in a monastic "drying tank" where he is sure he is being bugged by the higher-ups. So he attempts to negotiate his release by black-mailing the Church with all of its dirty secrets, big and small. The play was performed at RAPP, located in the former Most Holy Redeemer School, and drew a [[cease and desist]] order from the Catholic [[Archdiocese of New York]]. An article written by ''[[The New York Times]]''' Mervyn Rothstein got picked up around the world on the [[Associated Press|AP]] wire and the play became one of the most notable censorship controversies of the 1990s. After the [[American Civil Liberties Union]] declined to take the case, Disch and RAPP were represented by [[William Kunstler]] and [[Ron Kuby]], and the Archdiocese lost in court. Their response was to lock the theater out of their building and have the director jailed. Fortunately, ''The Cardinal Detoxes'' became as well known for its literary merits as for its controversy. It was selected for the compilations ''Best American Poetry 1994'' and ''Best of The Best American Poetry 1988–1997''.

In 1985, his short story "The Squirrel Cage", included in his book ''Fun with Your New Head'', was adapted for the stage by Robin Willoughby of Buffalo, New York. Music was composed by Tim Kloth. A single character is held captive by some unknown entity. The performer is surrounded on stage by an unseen and unheard (by him) circle of musicians who play in reaction to his musings.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc935586/m1/2/|title = The Squirrel Cage|date = August 1985}}</ref>

===Poetry===
[[File:Thomas Disch.jpg|right|thumb|upright|At South Street Seaport on June 3, 2008]]

Disch's first published poems, under the byline Tom Disch, were written alongside the stories and novels which made his name in the 1960s. His poetry includes experiments within traditional forms, such as a collaborative [[sonnet]] cycle ''Highway Sandwiches'' with [[Marilyn Hacker]] and Charles Platt and ''[[Haiku]]s of an AmPart'', while others like ''The Dark Old House'' mix stricter and freer form.

Disch's reputation as a poet was solidified by a 1989 midcareer retrospective collection, titled ''Yes, Let's''. A book of new poetry, ''Dark Verses & Light'', followed in 1991. In 1995 and 2002, Disch published two collections of poetry criticism. He continued to regularly publish poetry in magazines and journals such as ''Poetry'', ''Light'', ''Paris Review'', ''Partisan Review'', ''Parnassus: Poetry in Review'' and even ''Theology Today'' (perhaps an odd choice for a long-lapsed Catholic). Disch's poems were anthologized in four editions of ''The Best American Poetry''—those edited by John Ashbery, Jorie Graham, A. R. Ammons, and John Hollander.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bestamericanpoetry.com/archive/#|title = The Best American Poetry Series &#124; Series Archive}}</ref> Disch published two collections of poetry criticism, ''The Castle of Indolence: On Poetry, Poets, and Poetasters'' and ''The Castle of Perseverance: Job Opportunities in Contemporary Poetry''. His poetry criticism focuses on what makes poetry work, what makes it popular, and how poetry can re-establish its place in modern popular culture.

Near the end of his life he stopped submitting poetry to literary journals unless the journals asked for his contributions. He preferred to publish his poems in his LiveJournal account. In an interview ten days before his death, Disch said, "I write poetry because I think it is the hardest thing I can do well. And so I simply enjoy the doing of it, as an equestrian enjoys spending time on a good horse. Poetry is my good horse."<ref>{{citation |title=Podcast Interview: Thomas M. Disch |first=Edward |last=Champion |url=http://www.edrants.com/segundo/thomas-m-disch-bss-219/ |periodical=The Bat Segundo Show |date=June 25, 2008}}</ref>
